articles.title: Enhancing diagnostic and intervention-related skills with adaptive feedback: Study protocol for a simulation-based learning study on symptoms of learning and behavioural difficulties.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: This project uses simulated digital case scenarios to analyse diagnostic and intervention-related skills of teacher, school psychology, and medical students concerning primary school children's difficulties in mathematics and their hyperactive, inattentive and impulsive behaviours. Here, the conditions for an effective use of macro- and micro-adaptive feedback - powered by natural language processing (NLP) methods - compared to static feedback will be the focus. The aim is to identify effective types of feedback for students who differ in their prior diagnostic and intervention-related knowledge.
METHODS/DESIGN: We compare three groups of university students (medical students, school psychology students, and pre-service teachers) with varying professional specialisations and corresponding knowledge bases as learning prerequisites using simulated digital case scenarios. In validation study 1a, we analyse students' case processing and validate our measures for students' prior knowledge. Furthermore, the results are used for informing the design and refinement of micro- and macro-adaptive feedback. Validation study 1b investigates static, macro-adaptive, and micro-adaptive feedback. In Study 2, by using "think aloud"-methods and trace data, we investigate to what extent learners benefit differently from the processing of digital case scenarios in the absence of any feedback and what kind of cognitive, metacognitive, motivational learning processes occur. In study 3, we investigate how the form of feedback in the digital case scenarios affects students' acquisition of new diagnostic and intervention-related skills and how students process the different forms of feedback. Finally, Study 4 examines the extent to which different forms of feedback are helpful for students with low vs. high prior knowledge.
DISCUSSION: This project will analyse which benefits feedback with different degrees of adaptivity can provide for learning diagnostic reasoning and the planning of related interventions, especially when considering potential interaction effects with learners' varying prior professional as well as diagnostic and intervention-related knowledge and diagnostic processing.

articles.title: Caring for Patients Anywhere, Anyhow: How Emergency Department Crowding and Boarding Shapes Professional Identity in Emergency Medicine Training.
articles.journal: The western journal of emergency medicine
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Emergency department (ED) boarding is a well-documented crisis associated with adverse patient outcomes, healthcare worker burnout, and moral injury. Although prior work has documented operational and educational impacts, including reductions in resident productivity and procedural exposure, less is known about how sustained boarding shapes professional identity formation. We sought to explore how sustained ED boarding shapes the learning experiences and professional identity formation of emergency medicine (EM) residents, as perceived by both residents and the attending physicians who train them.
METHODS: Using a constructivist paradigm, we conducted a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with residents and attending physicians from a 4-year EM residency program with rotations across 5 clinical sites, between July and August 2025. Two researchers independently coded transcripts and iteratively refined a shared codebook, continuing until additional interviews were unlikely to add new insight, guided by the concept of information power. We used reflexive thematic analysis, treating researchers' clinical and analytic judgment as a resource for identifying patterns of meaning, and prioritized participants' own construction of meaning over the frequency of any single idea, consistent with an interpretive phenomenological approach.
RESULTS: We interviewed 13 emergency physicians: 6 residents and 7 attending physicians (range: 1-30+ years after residency). Three overarching themes emerged: (1) Educational challenges and opportunities-boarding fragments diagnostic ownership, narrows the acuity spectrum, and limits authentic undifferentiated encounters, although attending physicians adapt through structured hypotheticals and micro-teaching); (2) Shifts in the clinical environment-operational and structural adaptations create educational dead space, constrain the therapeutic alliance, and generate role ambiguity around boarded patients); and (3) Moral strain and suffering-moral injury and combined suffering is not peripheral to training but embedded within it, shaping how residents interpret professional responsibility and integrity. The three themes exist in a triangular relationship, with suffering at the foundation.
CONCLUSION: Boarding appeared to function as a formative context for professional identity formation, not merely a disruptive one. Residents described learning systems-level practice, advocacy, and emotional regulation, often through loss and moral injury, alongside attending physicians navigating the same. These findings suggest that recognizing boarding as a structural condition of training may reorient the responsibility of graduate medical education: formalizing adaptive teaching strategies, creating structured opportunities to process moral strain, and committing to advocacy that treats boarding as the educational crisis it is.

articles.title: Feasibility and perceived educational value of extended reality trauma simulation for emergency medical teams in a multinational training context.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Large-scale civil military medical live simulation exercises such as NATO Centre of Excellence for Military Medicine's (NATO MILMED COE) Vigorous Warrior (VW) series provide authentic environments to test interoperability and clinical performance of Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs). However, such exercises are resource intensive, logistically demanding, and infrequent, raising challenges for sustained workforce readiness. Extended Reality (XR) has emerged as a complementary modality with potential to extend access to trauma training, reduce costs, and support distributed learning. This study aimed to examine the educational feasibility of XR trauma simulation when embedded in multinational large scale live simulation.
METHODS: We conducted an educational feasibility study during Vigorous Warrior 2024 in Hungary, embedded within NATO MILMED COE's multinational large scale medical live simulation. Twenty-five EMT members from three countries (physicians, anaesthesiologists, nurses, and radiographers) participated in an XR-based penetrating chest trauma scenario using the MilExTS XR platform (Meta Quest 3 headset). Feasibility outcomes were evaluated across recruitment, implementation, usability, acceptability and perceived educational value using session logs, post-simulation surveys (Likert scales 1-5), and open-ended qualitative feedback. Data were analysed descriptively and thematically, in line with published feasibility frameworks for medical education.
RESULTS: Recruitment and completion thresholds were fully achieved (100% participation, 100% survey completion). Acceptability was high, with 88% of participants rating XR as good or excellent for trauma training and indicating willingness to use it in future education. Two-thirds (66%) endorsed XR for enhancing teamwork, while 68% valued opportunities for individual decision-making practice in a safe environment. Usability findings were mixed: 56% of participants rated scenario realism as average or below, cited limited physiological fidelity, lack of tactile feedback, headset navigation challenges, and insufficient role differentiation. Qualitative data supported XR's perceived educational value while identifying areas requiring further technological and pedagogical development.
CONCLUSION: XR trauma simulation demonstrated educational feasibility, high acceptability, and perceived learning value when embedded within a complex multinational large scale live simulation exercise. While limitations in realism and interface design remain, XR shows promise as a complementary modality for interprofessional trauma training. Further research should progress to efficacy testing, cost-effective analysis and curricular integration before wider adoption.

articles.title: Integrating U.S. embassy visits into global health education: student reflections on diplomacy-focused experiential learning.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: U.S. embassy visits offer a unique opportunity to examine the intersection of diplomacy and healthcare yet are rarely incorporated into health professions education. This study examined student reflections following a U.S. Embassy visit in North Macedonia to inform the integration of diplomacy-focused experiential learning into global health curricula.
METHODS: Twenty-one Ohio State University undergraduates (12 females; mean age=19.48±0.60 years) participated in an experiential learning activity at the U.S. Embassy-Skopje, North Macedonia, which included discussions with embassy personnel on diplomacy and healthcare delivery within a diplomatic setting, as well as an Embassy Health Unit tour. Immediately following the visit, students completed a structured written reflection describing a meaningful or surprising aspect of the experience and its influence on their understanding of diplomacy, healthcare, or international collaboration. Reflections were analyzed using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis. Themes were developed through iterative coding and refinement, with the second author independently reviewing the thematic framework to confirm interpretations and achieve consensus.
RESULTS: Reflexive thematic analysis identified three major themes-Expanding Conceptions of Diplomacy and the U.S. Foreign Service, Recognizing Healthcare as a Diplomatic Enterprise, and Broadening Professional Identity through Exposure to Global Health Careers-each comprising two related subthemes.
DISCUSSION: Student reflections highlighted adaptability, resilience, cross-cultural communication, teamwork, and flexibility while revealing progression from knowledge to understanding to professional identity. The embassy visit expanded students' understanding of diplomacy while introducing previously unrecognized career pathways. Drawing on these findings, we propose a conceptual framework comprising four interconnected learning domains, suggesting that embassy visits provide a valuable component of global health education abroad.

articles.title: Evaluating learning formats in international collaborative nursing education on professional agency in perioperative sustainability: protocol for a mixed-methods, randomised pilot study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Perioperative care is a highly resource-intensive component of healthcare, with operating theatres consuming substantial energy and generating considerable waste and emissions. Sustainable perioperative practice is therefore essential to reduce environmental impact. However, there is limited understanding of how competencies in sustainable practice can be developed within operating theatre nursing education. In particular, little attention has been given to how educational interventions shape students’ professional agency in relation to sustainability. Collaborative Online International Learning (COIL) offers a pedagogical approach that supports reflective and intercultural learning and may offer opportunities to foster professional agency for sustainability. This protocol describes a mixed-methods, randomised, feasibility pilot study that aims to assess the feasibility and acceptability of implementing and evaluating two learning formats in international collaborative learning in theatre nursing education, while also generating preliminary insights into how these formats may influence students’ reflective work and expressions of professional agency.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: A 90-minute synchronous online seminar focusing on sustainable theatre nursing practice across perioperative care phases will be delivered as part of the curriculum to operating theatre nursing students at Karolinska Institutet (Sweden) and Oslo Metropolitan University (Norway). Students will be randomly allocated (1:1) to one of two formats: (1) phase-specific COIL, in which small groups focus on a single perioperative phase, followed by whole-group sharing across phases, with documentation in a digital space; or (2) cross-phase COIL, in which small groups address all phases, document their work using a self-selected format and subsequently engage in whole-group comparison. A pragmatic sample of 24–36 students is anticipated. Primary outcomes are feasibility and acceptability indicators, including consent rates, questionnaire completion and follow-up rates, intervention fidelity, participant engagement and the feasibility of repeated questionnaire administration. Qualitative data, including collaborative outputs and observer field notes, will be analysed using reflexive thematic analysis informed by a conceptual model of professional agency and sustainability competence. Comparative analyses will explore differences in the complexity of students’ expressions of professional agency across learning formats. Quantitative data will include students’ perceptions of intercultural collaboration and learning, as well as attitudes towards sustainability in the operating theatre, assessed before the seminar and 1 week later. Because questionnaire responses are anonymous and cannot be linked at the individual level, baseline and follow-up data will be analysed as independent aggregate datasets. Quantitative findings will therefore be interpreted descriptively and will not be used to assess individual-level changes over time. Integration of qualitative and quantitative findings will be conducted at the interpretation stage using a triangulation approach.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: The study has been approved by the Norwegian Agency for Shared Services in Education and Research (reference number 266740). In Sweden, the study was reviewed by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (reference number 2026-00252-01), which concluded that the study did not require formal ethical approval under the Swedish Ethical Review Act and issued an advisory opinion. Participation in the research component is voluntary, and informed consent will be obtained. All data will be de-identified prior to analysis. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations and will inform the design of a future randomised controlled trial (RCT) of an educational intervention aimed at supporting sustainable practice in operating theatre nursing education.
STUDY REGISTRATION: Open Science Framework (OSF; 10.17605/OSF.IO/YMF6V). Protocol version: 2.0 (23 September 2026), incorporating clarifications made prior to intervention delivery and outcome data collection.

articles.title: Point-of-care ultrasound use in the Canadian Armed Forces: Current practices, barriers, and opportunities for integration.
articles.journal: Journal of military, veteran and family health
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) enables real-time diagnostic imaging to support clinical decision-making and procedural safety. Its use is particularly relevant in military environments, where access to conventional imaging is often limited or unavailable. This study assessed current POCUS use, training and perceived barriers among Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) clinicians to guide future integration across clinical and operational contexts.
METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was distributed to CAF clinicians between Sep. 6 and Nov. 24, 2024. The survey collected data on clinician demographics, POCUS training, device access, clinical applications, frequency of use, perceived barriers, and preferred modalities of future instruction. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize survey responses. The study received ethics approval from the Montfort Hospital Research Ethics Board and endorsement from the Surgeon General Health Research Program.
RESULTS: A total of 112 clinicians completed the survey. Respondents included medical officers (61%), medical specialist officers (17%), physician assistants (16%), and nurse practitioners (6%). Prior POCUS training was reported by 73% of respondents, primarily through civilian courses and peer-led instruction. Only 59% reported current access to a POCUS device. Trauma (95%), cardiac (76%), and lung (72%) assessments were the most common applications. Barriers included limited device access (58%), insufficient training (41%), skill decay, and absence of institutional standards. POCUS use varied by clinical role and was less frequent in operational deployments.
DISCUSSION: This study identified variability in POCUS training, access, and use across the CAF. A coordinated strategy involving clinical and non-clinical stakeholders may support more consistent implementation across CAF health care settings.

articles.title: Educators' insights on integrating artificial intelligence into medical curricula: a qualitative study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming medical education by offering innovative solutions for teaching and learning. However, integrating AI into medical curricula, particularly in low-resource settings like Sudan, presents both unique challenges and promising opportunities. The current research aimed to provide actionable insights for implementing AI in resource-constrained contexts.
OBJECTIVES: This study explores the perceptions of educators regarding AI integration in medical education, focusing on challenges, opportunities, and actionable strategies in resource-constrained environments.
METHODOLOGY: A qualitative design was employed, involving 24 semi-structured interviews with educators from diverse backgrounds. Data were analyzed using Clarke's six-step thematic analysis framework.
RESULTS: Five key themes emerged: perceptions of AI in medical education, challenges in AI integration, opportunities for curriculum development and collaboration, teaching strategies for AI adoption, and recommendations for implementation. Educators highlighted the transformative potential of AI while identifying barriers such as infrastructure limitations, faculty expertise gaps, and ethical concerns. Opportunities included enhancing teaching and research, fostering global collaborations, and embedding AI into curricula.
CONCLUSION: Effective integration of AI in medical education requires addressing resource constraints, improving faculty training, and embedding ethical considerations. This study provides actionable insights for leveraging AI to advance medical education, particularly in low-resource settings.

articles.title: Active duty service members' experiences navigating musculoskeletal health throughout their military careers: a qualitative interview study.
articles.journal: Frontiers in sports and active living
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Musculoskeletal injury (MSK-I) and pain (MSK-P) pose a substantial burden to Active Duty Service Members (ADSM) and are a leading cause of medical encounters and lost duty days. Evidence indicates that barriers exist to musculoskeletal (MSK) health care-seeking, which can result in exacerbation of MSK conditions (e.g., MSK-I, MSK-P), chronic pain, and greater healthcare costs. The objective of this qualitative study was to interview ADSM about their experiences navigating MSK health during their military careers to inform the development of tools and resources that better equip ADSM and military medical providers to prevent and manage MSK conditions.
METHODS: Semi-structured individual interviews were conducted with male and female ADSM (n = 60). Interviews assessed ADSMs' experiences with MSK-I/P during military service, the use of military resources to maintain MSK health, and barriers and facilitators to seeking care for MSK-I/P. Interviews lasted 20-60 min, were conducted in-person or over video conference, and were audio recorded and transcribed. Transcript data were analyzed using applied thematic analysis (ATA).
RESULTS: Participants included male (n = 31) and female (n = 29) ADSM (age=38 ± 10 years, 16 ± 9 years of service) representing all military branches except for the Space Force. The ATA resulted in seven themes: military impact, care-seeking, Military Health System (MHS), prevention and optimization, leadership, mental health, and gender.
DISCUSSION: ADSM revealed that while the military culture promotes physical fitness, it also encourages a "push through pain" mentality, leading to delayed care due to fears of career repercussions or being seen as weak or a burden to one's unit. Additionally, ADSM pointed to certain challenges within the MHS, including long wait times, inconsistent access to specialized care, and a perception that some providers dismiss ADSM pain. Results revealed additional areas of investigation and intervention, such as a bidirectional link between MSK-P and mental health, and identified gender-specific challenges, such as a lack of resources for women's health issues like postpartum MSK conditions. Overall, the findings identified opportunities for systemic and cultural changes to destigmatize MSK issues, prioritize prevention and proactive care-seeking, and improve healthcare access for MSK conditions during military service.

articles.title: Specialty-Driven Divergence in Cardiac Imaging (Coronary Computed Tomography Angiography and Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography) Utilization Following the 2021 Chest Pain Guideline at a Large Military Medical Center.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) received a strong recommendation in the 2021 Chest Pain Guideline as a first-line test for the evaluation of stable chest pain in patients without known coronary artery disease; however, real-world adoption remains variable. Within the Military Health System, imaging decisions directly affect operational readiness. We evaluated changes in the utilization of CCTA versus single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) myocardial perfusion imaging before and after guideline publication at a large military medical center.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 15,772 CCTA or SPECT studies performed for the evaluation of suspected coronary artery disease from 2018 through 2023 at Joint Base San Antonio. Studies were stratified into pre-guideline (on or before October 31, 2021) and post-guideline (on or after November 1, 2021) periods. The primary outcome was imaging modality (CCTA versus SPECT), analyzed by ordering specialty, sex, and age. Chi-square testing, repeat-testing characterization, and generalized estimating equations logistic regression were performed.
RESULTS: Overall, 41.3% of studies were CCTA and 58.7% were SPECT. Among cardiologists, the proportion of CCTA studies increased from 50% to 61% after guideline publication, whereas CCTA use among non-cardiology specialties declined from 36% to 25%, reaching a quarterly nadir of 12.6% in quarter 2 of 2022. Cardiology ordering was the strongest independent predictor of CCTA use (odds ratio 1.90, 95% CI, 1.76-2.05; P < .001). The post-guideline period alone was not independently associated with increased CCTA use (odds ratio 0.98, P = .69). Younger age strongly favored CCTA, and repeat testing most commonly involved SPECT-to-SPECT sequences.
CONCLUSIONS: Publication of the 2021 Chest Pain Guideline was not associated with a uniform increase in CCTA adoption. Provider specialty, rather than the guideline period itself, was the dominant factor associated with modality selection, highlighting the need for targeted education and decision-support interventions to improve evidence-based imaging utilization.

articles.title: Defensive adoption and the intermediate coding threshold in generative AI usage among medical postgraduates: a cross-sectional mixed-methods study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in medical research presents both methodological opportunities and pedagogical challenges. While traditional technology acceptance models characterize anxiety as a barrier to adoption, high-pressure academic environments may instead foster a "defensive adoption" mechanism. This study investigates the structural relationships among AI anxiety, agentic literacy, and usage intentions, and identifies distinct user profiles among medical postgraduates.
METHODS: This cross-sectional mixed-methods study analyzed 414 valid responses from medical postgraduates in China. The self-developed Agentic Literacy scale underwent expert content validation, cognitive interviews, and pilot testing prior to the main survey. The analytical framework comprised two stages. First, structural equation modeling (SEM) tested the hypothesized causal pathways, while controlling for prior programming experience. Second, latent profile analysis (LPA) identified heterogeneous subgroups based on user patterns. Quantitative findings were triangulated with a qualitative thematic analysis of open-ended responses to capture the cognitive mechanisms underlying different adoption profiles.
RESULTS: Participants primarily engaged with GenAI for basic text processing, with 17.4% utilizing tools for deep methodological tasks. SEM analysis indicated a pattern consistent with defensive adoption, where higher AI anxiety was associated with greater intention to use GenAI ([Formula: see text] = 0.254, P < 0.001). Furthermore, deeper use was associated with higher agentic literacy, which emerged as the strongest observed correlate for crossing the intermediate coding threshold. LPA identified three distinct profiles: Agentic Innovators (high literacy, high anxiety), Moderate Adopters, and Detached Users (low literacy, low anxiety). Qualitative analysis revealed that "Detached Users" focused on safety and hallucination auditing, whereas "Agentic Innovators" leveraged AI for complex code orchestration, confirming that anxiety was associated with adoption only when paired with competency.
CONCLUSION: In this cross-sectional sample, higher academic AI anxiety was associated with stronger intention to use GenAI, while deeper use was more closely associated with agentic literacy. Surpassing the intermediate coding threshold may require specific training in AI orchestration rather than mere technological access.

articles.title: Metacognitive team-based learning for creative problem-solving in Indian medical undergraduates: a single-arm pre-post quasi-experimental mixed-methods study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Metacognitive and team-based strategies can strengthen problem-solving; however, many Indian medical undergraduates remain reliant on rote memorisation with limited exposure to structured, creativity-focused pedagogy. Structured interventions combining metacognitive training with collaborative, multidisciplinary teaching remain scarce in Indian undergraduate medical education. This study aimed to design, implement, and evaluate the Creative Problem-Solving Skills through Metacognition (CPSSM) module, a novel three-phase intervention for first-year MBBS students.
METHODS: A single-arm, pre-post, quasi-experimental, mixed-methods study was conducted at AIIMS Rajkot, India, during the 2024-2025 academic year. After obtaining ethical clearance and prospective trial registration, all 50 first-year MBBS students were recruited by universal sampling and 49 completed the intervention. Participants underwent three sequential phases: integrated teaching, case-based discussion, and collaborative model-making, delivered by a multidisciplinary faculty team. They were allocated to ten heterogeneous groups by stratified, non-random allocation based on baseline Metacognitive Awareness Inventory cut-off bands. The pre-specified primary outcome was post-intervention problem-solving accuracy, and the secondary outcomes included self-perceived creativity, group metacognition, and domain knowledge. Quantitative data were analysed using t-tests and ANOVA, with effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals. Qualitative feedback was analysed using descriptive content analysis informed by the Braun and Clarke thematic framework. No comparison group was included; therefore, the findings are reported as associations rather than causal effects.
RESULTS: Students with high baseline metacognitive awareness showed a significant within-group gain in problem-solving accuracy (28.59 to 30.87; mean difference = 2.28; p < 0.001; Cohen's d = 1.53); the moderate-awareness group's gain was smaller and non-significant. Female students outperformed males in problem-solving accuracy at both time points (pre-test: p < 0.01, d = 0.90). Self-perceived creativity was higher in the high metacognition group than in the moderate-metacognition group (59.09 vs. 52.72; p = 0.01). Thematic analysis identified teamwork, motivation, and growing confidence as the principal perceived gains, alongside coordination and resource-related challenges. Creativity was rarely cited spontaneously, despite being a primary intended outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: Participation in the CPSSM module was associated with modest gains in problem-solving accuracy, which was most evident among students with stronger baseline metacognitive awareness. These findings support the feasibility of structured, metacognition-driven, team-based learning in early medical education; however, controlled, multi-site studies are needed before broader effectiveness can be claimed.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinical Trials Registry-India, CTRI/2025/02/080559. This study was registered prospectively on February 14, 2025.

articles.title: From technique to sensitivity: the transformation of clinical and ethical reasoning in physiotherapy students in the context of chronic neurodegenerative diseases.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The evolution of Physiotherapy requires a shift from the biomedical model towards bioethical and humanistic approaches. This study explores how final-year students perceive their professional role when dealing with patients with complex neurodegenerative conditions, where traditional technical success is challenged by the irreversibility of the deterioration.
METHODS: Qualitative research based on interpretative description. Thirty final-year students from the University of Almería (Spain) took part, divided into five working groups. Three training sessions and discussions were held on Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), Alzheimer's disease, stroke and Rett syndrome. The data were analysed using thematic analysis and triangulation by researchers external to the study, with reflexivity ensured through logbooks.
RESULTS: A shift in clinical reasoning was identified, with sensitivity taking precedence over technique. Students redefined therapeutic success in terms of "comfort" and support, valuing "microscopic achievements" such as the preservation of dignity and the alleviation of distress. Of particular note is the ability to adapt ethical principles according to the patient's cognitive integrity (autonomy in ALS versus protection in Alzheimer's) and the integration of the carer as an inseparable part of the therapeutic process.
CONCLUSION: Future physiotherapists perceive humanization and the empathetic interpretation of non-verbal cues as essential therapeutic tools. Unlike previous studies focused on clinical experience, this research explores pre-clinical ethical maturation, offering a unique perspective on the educational foundation and humanistic predisposition of future graduates prior to their immersion in the healthcare system. It is imperative that academic curricula formally integrate competencies in bioethics, palliative care and emotional management to prepare graduates for extreme vulnerability and prevent early professional burnout.

articles.title: Sweet Success: Using Candy Land to Explore Gamification in Medical Education.
articles.journal: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine
articles.abstract:
AUDIENCE: This session is intended for learners and educators interested in medical education, including medical students, residents, fellows, and faculty.
INTRODUCTION: Gamification is increasingly recognized as an effective strategy to enhance engagement, motivation, and active learning in medical education. Despite its potential, many educators are unsure how to implement gamified strategies effectively. This session demonstrates a practical, interactive approach to applying gamification principles in a collaborative educational setting.
EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES: By the end of this session, learners will be able to (1) describe key principles of gamification in medical education, (2) identify resources and tools for implementing gamification, (3) actively participate in a gamified educational activity, and (4) design a simple plan to implement gamification in their own teaching, considering benefits and potential challenges.
EDUCATIONAL METHODS: The session started with brief didactic lecture on game-based learning and gamification intended to orient participants to the material. Participants then engaged in a Candy Land-inspired, team-based activity. Twenty-five prompts covering aspects of gamification were arranged along a winding pathway drawn with chalk. Teams of 3-4 learners advanced along the path by rolling a large inflatable die and answering questions or discussing scenarios associated with the prompts. Correct answers earned points or allowed teams to advance, while debriefing discussions linked gameplay to the principles and strategies of gamification. Incorrect answers were not penalized. This approach leveraged experiential learning, active learning, and social constructivist principles to support both knowledge acquisition and practical application.
RESEARCH METHODS: The session was evaluated through direct observation and informal feedback from learners and instructors. Engagement, discussion quality, and participation were used as primary indicators of effectiveness. Modifications and recommendations for future implementation were derived from observed challenges and learner feedback.
RESULTS: Fifteen learners of varied training levels participated. Observations indicated high engagement, lively discussion, and collaborative problem-solving. Feedback was universally positive, with learners reporting increased confidence in understanding gamification principles and motivation to apply these strategies in their own teaching. Several participants subsequently incorporated gamified activities into educational sessions in the following weeks. Key lessons for implementation included ensuring sufficient space, clarifying scoring systems, and preparing materials in advance.
DISCUSSION: This session demonstrates that gamification can effectively engage learners across multiple levels, promote collaborative learning, and provide practical insights into implementation strategies. Learners experienced the mechanics and benefits of gamification firsthand, while also reflecting on challenges and planning for real-world application. The activity highlights how structured games can create a safe and inclusive learning environment, fostering participation from all learners. Future iterations may further optimize space, scoring, and team organization to enhance learning outcomes.
TOPICS: Gamification in medical education, game-based learning, interactive learning strategies, experiential learning, social constructivism, educational game design, team-based learning, implementation strategies, engagement and motivation, active learning.

articles.title: All In: A Casino-Themed Emergency Medicine Conference Day.
articles.journal: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine
articles.abstract:
AUDIENCE: The target audience includes individuals involved in the education and training of emergency medicine (EM) residents, such as program directors, assistant program directors, core faculty, and academic attendings, as well as learners including residents, physician assistant (PA) fellows, and medical students (MS).
INTRODUCTION: Gamification has increasingly been incorporated into emergency medicine (EM) residency education to enhance learner engagement, motivation, and active participation. Prior studies have demonstrated benefits of game-based learning across multiple areas of medical education, including improved knowledge retention, teamwork, communication, and learner satisfaction.1-4 However, most gamification interventions in EM involve isolated activities rather than comprehensive, multi-station conference curricula. To address this gap, we developed a casino-themed, multi-station educational conference designed to reinforce core EM knowledge, procedural skills, and clinical reasoning through competitive, team-based learning. The intervention incorporated simulation, rapid-response scenarios, board-style trivia, and wagering poker chips during a protected half-day residency conference.
EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES: By the end of this educational intervention, participants will be able to: 1) demonstrate airway management skills through simulation, including equipment setup and timely interventions for both adult and pediatric cases, 2) interpret various electrocardiograms (EKGs) in high-pressure scenarios, 3) analyze cases and apply evidence-based management in various rapid-response scenarios, 4) demonstrate rapid recall of EM knowledge by answering board-style trivia questions, and 5) demonstrate increased confidence in team-based decision-making, effective communication under pressure, and leadership in high-stress emergency situations.
EDUCATIONAL METHODS: This prospective educational innovation was delivered as a single, four-hour casino-themed EM conference session featuring interactive stations modeled after casino games and held during the residency program's weekly Wednesday educational conference. The session featured interactive, competition-based stations designed to replicate high-pressure ED scenarios. Learners rotated through four game-based stations: "Play Your Cards Right" for rapid-recall trivia using EM board-style questions, "Diagnostic Craps" for EKG interpretation and management, "High Stakes Airways" for hands-on airway management using mannequins and rapid sequence intubation scenarios, and "Rapid Response Roulette" for discussion of ED cases focusing on team dynamics, leadership, resuscitation, and escalation of care. The games were designed to reflect real-world ED challenges, with content and expectations tailored to postgraduate years (PGY) levels. Participants wagered poker chips based on confidence in their responses, reinforcing self-assessment and accountability. This method encouraged active participation, peer-to-peer learning, and application of clinical reasoning in high-pressure scenarios.
RESEARCH METHODS: The casino-style conference featured six tables each with an EM attending facilitator. Participants included EM residents, physician assistant (PA) fellows, and medical students. Learners started with 15 poker chips and engaged in four game-based sessions over four hours. The games "Play Your Cards Right," "High Stakes Airways," "Diagnostic Craps," and "Rapid Response Roulette" incorporated either case-based simulation, procedural skill stations, rapid decision-making, EKG interpretation, and/or evidence-based medicine (EBM) trivia. Learners wagered chips based on confidence, with gains/losses tied to performance. Faculty provided real-time feedback and facilitated discussions. Pre- and post-conference surveys (Appendix A) assessed educational value, skill improvement, confidence, and clinical applicability. Instructors also evaluated feasibility and effectiveness. The study was Institutional Review Board exempt.
RESULTS: Of the 33 learners who attended the conference, 32 completed surveys (97% response rate) including 26 EM residents (10 PGY-1, 8 PGY-2 and 8 PGY-3), 4 medical students, and 2 physician assistants. One hundred percent of participants answered "yes" when asked if they would recommend this type of conference to peers and 100% preferred this learning style to traditional didactics. Eighty-eight percent of the respondents reported they are "very likely" to incorporate skills learned from this activity into future practice.Facilitators rated the game-based learning activities as highly effective teaching tools, with 92% rating 4 or 5 (on a 5-point scale). Facilitators were also asked if they found the games easy to implement, and 83% answered rating a 4 or a 5 (on a 5-point scale). Responses derived from the open-ended questions emphasize the conference's effectiveness in engaging participants, providing meaningful learning experiences and fostering a positive and well-organized environment.
DISCUSSION: This casino-style, game-based learning conference was highly rated for both educational value and engagement. Participants reported increased confidence in managing emergency scenarios, particularly in EKG interpretation and team-based critical decision-making. The format was viewed as feasible and effective, with most participants preferring game-based learning over traditional didactics, supporting its continued use in EM education.
TOPICS: Gamification, EM education, simulation, active learning, residency training.

articles.title: Meeting the Milestones through Simulation: Disclosing a Medical Error.
articles.journal: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine
articles.abstract:
AUDIENCE: This simulation is intended for medical students, interns, junior residents, and senior residents.
INTRODUCTION: Patient safety event reporting and disclosure of medical errors to patients and families are critical components of high-quality, transparent care and a necessary skill for emergency medicine (EM) physicians. Accurate reporting of errors, near misses, and unsafe conditions provides institutions with the data needed to investigate vulnerabilities, implement system-based solutions, and prevent recurrence. Disclosure of medical errors fosters trust, supports just culture principles, and reinforces professional accountability.1 Physicians have historically reported few adverse events, accounting for only 1-2% of all reports.2 To address this gap, the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) now emphasizes patient safety and quality improvement as a part of resident education.The ACGME Emergency Medicine Milestones have established clear expectations for resident education in patient safety.3 Residents, fellows, and faculty must know their responsibilities for event reporting. The milestones include ability to identify patient safety events, understand the system factors that lead to events, and how to complete institutional safety event reports.3 ACGME requires residents to participate in real or simulated interprofessional patient safety events and quality improvement activities as part of systems-based practice milestones.3 These requirements underscore the importance of experiential learning, feedback, and practice in order to achieve true competence in identifying causes and enacting sustainable safety interventions.Medication errors, particularly dosing errors, are among the most common patient safety threats in the emergency department (ED).4 The ED environment-with high patient volumes, time-sensitive decision-making, and frequent weight-based dosing-places EM physicians at especially high risk for ordering or administering incorrect doses. In this simulation, the wrong concentration of a sedation medication is administered and creates a scenario in which the learner must recognize the error, disclose it to the patient/family, and complete a patient safety report (PSR). This approach integrates clinical management with communication and systems-based practice and provides an avenue for residency programs to facilitate ACGME requirements while preparing residents for real-world patient safety responsibilities in scenarios that otherwise may not yet be encountered during the period of residency.
EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES: By the end of this simulation activity, learners will be able to: 1) disclose a medical error to a patient and/or their family, 2) understand the different types of patient safety events that should be reported, 3) locate the form for disclosing a patient safety event at their institution, and 4) appropriately complete a patient safety report at their institution.
EDUCATIONAL METHODS: The simulation was conducted with a high-fidelity pediatric mannikin. A total of 19 residents and three medical students participated in the simulation during their monthly didactic session. Afterwards, they were guided through completing a patient safety report for their institution.
RESEARCH METHODS: Learners completed a survey before and after the simulation case assessing their comfort with disclosing medical errors and completing an institutional patient safety report form. The survey questions were formatted in a Likert scale where 1 = strongly disagree, 2 = disagree, 3 = neither agree nor disagree, 4 = agree, 5 = strongly agree. Results collected were analyzed using Wilcox rank-sum test.
RESULTS: The participants completed a survey before and after the experience, and there was a statistically significant improvement in the learners' comfort level after completing the simulation. The free text responses were also universally positive.
DISCUSSION: Overall, the learners received the simulation well. General feedback was positive; the consensus was that there was increased confidence in patient safety reporting.
TOPICS: Patient safety, medical error, disclosing error.

articles.title: A Low-Cost Rectal Foreign Body Removal Simulator.
articles.journal: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine
articles.abstract:
AUDIENCE: This rectal foreign body removal model is designed to instruct emergency medicine residents. However, the innovation is appropriate for medical students, advanced practice providers (APPs), attending physicians, and clinicians in other medical specialties.
INTRODUCTION: Rectal foreign bodies are relatively uncommon emergency department presentations but are associated with significant morbidity and mortality.1 These foreign bodies require prompt recognition and skilled management, which can be challenging due to stigma, patient discomfort, and procedural complexity. Learners often have limited opportunities for hands-on experience with rectal foreign body removal, and to our knowledge, no established simulation tool currently exists for training in this procedure. This task trainer was designed as an easily assembled, cost-effective simulation tool to support procedural practice and promote safe, effective performance when applied in the emergency department setting.
EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES: This task trainer is intended to facilitate hands-on training in rectal foreign body removal. By the end of this training session, learners should be able to: 1) describe the indications and contraindications for rectal foreign body removal in the emergency department, and 2) demonstrate the ability to remove rectal foreign bodies of varying sizes, shapes, and depths of insertion using multiple techniques.
EDUCATIONAL METHODS: This innovation consists of a task trainer for the simulated removal of rectal foreign bodies. The tool was constructed using readily available, inexpensive materials to accommodate the removal of foreign bodies of varying sizes and depths, allowing for customizable scenarios of variable difficulty. The session began with a brief didactic overview covering anatomy, tools, procedural steps, and complications of rectal foreign body removal, followed by supervised hands-on practice using the model. Faculty provided individualized feedback to help learners refine their techniques.
RESEARCH METHODS: A pre- and post-activity survey was administered to participants to assess comfort with rectal foreign body removal and gather feedback on the educational session and task trainer. The pre-activity survey asked learners to report the number of rectal foreign body removals they had performed and to rate their comfort with the procedure on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = totally comfortable, 7 = totally uncomfortable). The post-activity survey included the same comfort scale to allow for comparison, along with additional items evaluating the model and session. Learners rated the model's realism (1 = extremely realistic, 5 = not at all realistic), the degree to which the session increased their confidence performing the procedure (1 = extremely, 5 = not at all), and the overall usefulness of the model for teaching rectal foreign body removal (1 = extremely useful, 5 = not useful at all). This evaluation approach addressed the reaction and learning levels of the Kirkpatrick model.
RESULTS: Thirty-nine learners completed the pre-activity survey and 37 completed the post-activity survey. Most learners (79%) had never previously performed a rectal foreign body removal. Following the session, learners reported significant improvements in comfort with the procedure. The task trainer received favorable ratings for realism, educational usefulness, and its ability to build confidence in performing the procedure on real patients.
DISCUSSION: This educational session was both effective and well-received. Learners began with limited experience performing rectal foreign body removal, a procedure that may be infrequently encountered but carries significant risk. Providing a structured opportunity for supervised practice in a low-risk environment likely contributed to the observed improvements in reported comfort and confidence.Beyond numerical gains, this session highlighted an important educational gap: most learners have limited exposure to this procedure that they are likely to encounter in their careers, underscoring the need for accessible methods of training in rare procedures. The favorable feedback regarding realism, confidence, and usefulness suggests that even a simple model can provide meaningful educational value.The main takeaway is that this rectal foreign body removal task trainer offers a practical, reproducible approach to improving learner preparedness in managing a sensitive and technically challenging procedure in the emergency department setting.
TOPICS: Rectal foreign bodies, medical simulation, hands-on training, emergency medicine education, rare procedures.

articles.title: The Challenge of Critical Feedback: A Simulation-based Advanced Residents as Teachers Module.
articles.journal: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine
articles.abstract:
AUDIENCE: This is a simulation module intended to train residents at all levels in giving targeted, critical feedback to medical students on shift.
INTRODUCTION: Residents as teachers (RAT) curricula are an important component of graduate medical education for residents who teach medical students.1 Developing residents' skills in teaching, feedback, and supervision is therefore a critical component of training. Medical students receive a substantial portion of their clinical education from residents,2,3 and timely, specific feedback in the clinical setting improves learner performance and professional development.4 Despite the importance of these skills, residents have limited opportunities to practice delivering challenging feedback beyond introductory teaching experiences.5,6 This curriculum addresses that gap by providing simulation-based practice in identifying learner gaps and delivering targeted, critical feedback to medical students.
EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES: The purpose of this module was to provide a safe learning environment for residents to practice giving critical feedback to medical students. By the end of the session, residents will be able to 1) identify gaps in student proficiency through analysis of a simulated student's clinical performance as demonstrated by a simulated case presentation, 2) formulate specific feedback for student learners to target identified gaps, and 3) apply a newly learned strategy for providing feedback to a "student" during two simulation-based communication cases.
EDUCATIONAL METHODS: We developed two simulation communication cases wherein resident participants of all training years were placed in the roles of a simulated medical student and a simulated resident. Both roles are structured for resident participants only and the simulated student role was performed by another resident before the roles were then switched for the second case. This educational session was held in small groups during resident didactics with a facilitator present with each of the small group sessions. The first case involves a presentation of a patient with leg pain with an underlying diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis, and the second involves a presentation of a patient with chest pain with an underlying diagnosis of pulmonary embolism. Face sheet information gives the simulated student and simulated resident unexpectedly different perspectives, leading the simulated student to omit can't-miss diagnoses and requiring the resident to recognize an opportunity for feedback and practice delivering teaching points. The simulated student, played by another resident, is also invited to provide comments to their partner on the teaching strategies used during a facilitator-led debrief following the completion of each case.
RESEARCH METHODS: Twenty-one participants completed pre-and post- surveys to gauge comfort with teaching and providing feedback to medical students on shift. Participants ranked their perceived importance of a "Residents as Teachers" curriculum in their medical education. We used a paired t-test to assess the change in rating before and after the cases. Statistical calculations were done using Excel. Participants provided qualitative data through open-ended feedback comments.
RESULTS: Resident confidence in teaching medical students on shift increased from 3.65 to 3.9 (P=0.01), and confidence in giving critical feedback increased from 3.2 to 3.95 (P<0.001). The perceived importance of a "Residents as Teachers" curriculum was overall unchanged from 4.4 to 4.5 (P>0.2). Review of feedback comments demonstrated an overall positive experience and several requests to receive further training on effective teaching. One resident playing the role of a "student" shared that they felt it was particularly helpful to play the role of the student to understand their perspective better, and several comments included a request for further opportunities for practice in the future. One resident suggested providing additional teaching on how to approach teaching students of different levels of training.
DISCUSSION: The utilization of these modules was well-received by participants and proved to be an effective way to improve resident comfort in providing critical feedback and teaching medical students on shift. Providing the simulated student and simulated resident with divergent clinical perspectives allowed for a nuanced discussion regarding how the residents felt in their individual roles and their perceived efficacy of the feedback provided to the simulated student. Residents communicated that the cases were reflective of experiences they have had on shift and appreciated the ability to practice their skills in a safe environment. They reported overall satisfaction with the cases and a desire to use similar cases in the future.
TOPICS: Simulation, medical education, residents as teachers curriculum, feedback.

articles.title: It's useless, too much and no one cares: How students make sense of feeling unmotivated.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Despite concerns about declining motivation and disengagement in pre-clinical medical education, research has largely focused on identifying factors that influence students' motivation. Less is known about how students make sense of their educational experiences as unmotivating. We explored how pre-clinical medical students make sense of feeling unmotivated, focusing on how they construct meanings around their educational participation.
METHODS: We conducted an inductive qualitative study with 16 pre-clinical medical students. Participants created Rich Pictures depicting an experience of feeling unmotivated in the medical programme, followed by in-depth interviews. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis within a constructivist paradigm.
RESULTS: Students' sensemaking was strongly shaped by emotions. Boredom, confusion and overwhelm could initiate meanings of educational activities as useless, the educational environment as no one cares and the curriculum as too much. These meanings could make educational participation feel frustrating, futile and stressful and contributed to a transactional attitude in which students participated primarily in exchange for something that would help them progress through the programme, such as a grade.
CONCLUSION: We interpret feeling unmotivated as educational participation changing meaning: from participation in becoming the physician students envision to participation organised primarily around meeting institutional demands. Drawing on Communities of Practice, we understand this shift in relation to students' trajectories of becoming. Students' sensemaking was highly emotional and, in the absence of authentic medical practice, shaped by imagined futures. This perspective offers a different way of understanding student motivation and highlights the importance of educational experiences that help pre-clinical students experience their participation as meaningfully connected to becoming the physician they envision.

articles.title: Exploring the educational needs of transgender and non-binary healthcare among Polish medical students.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Given that the transgender and non-binary community now accounts for as much as 1.2% of the total population, they are becoming an increasingly visible subgroup of patients in the healthcare system. At the same time, research indicates that these patients often experience poorer treatment outcomes or have limited access to services. Discrepancies between medical education and subsequent patient care are addressed by incorporating comprehensive education into medical training. To the best of our knowledge, this is one of the first studies exploring healthcare students' needs regarding transgender healthcare content in medical education in Poland. The aim of the study is to investigate healthcare students' knowledge of and attitudes towards transgender and non-binary (TGNB) patients, their preparedness to provide healthcare for this population, and their perceived educational needs in this area.
METHODS: An online survey on educational needs in healthcare of TGNB people was disseminated through social media and posters with a QR code. The survey was anonymous and targeted healthcare students from Poland. For open-ended questions, an inductive thematic analysis was performed.
RESULTS: Two hundred and sixty-four students, from medical-related faculties, completed the questionnaire. Two hundred and thirty-two (87.9%) respondents admitted that they had not received any content on healthcare for TGNB patients during their studies to date. One hundred and sixty-one (61.0%) of the respondents believed that content on TGNB patient care should be included in the curriculum. Communication with patients (73.9%) was indicated as the most relevant issues in the care of TGNB patients. Respondents rated their knowledge and skills as lowest in surgical treatment (59.1%) and hormonal treatment (50.0%). One hundred and twenty students (45.5%) did not feel prepared to interact with TGNB patients.
CONCLUSIONS: Polish healthcare students express an interest in improving their knowledge and skills on the healthcare of TGNB patients. Implementing educational interventions is essential to reduce future gap in medical services access for these patients.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: The decision number of the Bioethical Committee of the Medical University of Lublin is KE/138/02/24, Date of determination February 29, 2024.

articles.title: Sustaining Problem-Based Learning (PBL) in medical programs: insights from two continents.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Problem-based learning (PBL) is a well-established approach in health-professions education, valued for promoting self-directed collaborative learning, but its implementation varies widely across contexts. Linköping University and Moi University have adopted PBL for decades despite facing challenges such as limited resources. This was a comparative study aiming to explore experience of first-year medical students and tutors regarding PBL in two universities in different continents.
METHODS: Four focus groups were conducted with tutors and students respectively, from Moi University and Linköping University. In total, 24 participants were included. Data was analyzed using thematic analysis.
RESULTS: A prominent main theme was identified: system support for upholding the principles of PBL. Within this theme, five subthemes were developed unravelling various understandings of the core principles of PBL, as well as practices of PBL. The role of tutors was considered crucial, although their prerequisites and systemic support were not always sufficient. The findings highlight how clarity of procedures requires solid and committed leadership on various levels for a successful PBL process.
CONCLUSIONS: PBL supports active, collaborative learning, but its sustainability depends on having adequate institutional support. Without clear leadership, adequate resources, and ongoing competence development, the PBL principles risk being diluted over time.

articles.title: Assessment of knowledge and clinical experience with noma among healthcare professionals in Latin America: A cross-sectional survey.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Noma (cancrum oris) is a rapidly progressive necrotizing orofacial disease with high mortality and severe sequelae. Despite historical reports in Latin America, current awareness among healthcare professionals and case detection remain unknown.
OBJECTIVE: To assess the knowledge of noma among healthcare professionals, and explore reported clinical experiences, including suspected case encounters, differential diagnoses, outcomes, and barriers to care in Peru, Bolivia, Colombia, Brazil, and Mexico.
METHODS: A cross-sectional online survey was conducted for six months in 2025 and targeted physicians, oral health professionals, nurses, public health professionals, and community health workers. The questionnaire assessed demographics, noma knowledge (0-9 score), prior case encounters, differential diagnoses, comorbidities, treatment, and barriers. Open-ended responses underwent thematic analysis.
RESULTS: Of 401 respondents, 35% reported prior awareness of noma. Among these respondents, the median knowledge score was 70% (6.3/9), and 43% achieved an optimal knowledge level of 75%. Only 37% were aware of the high mortality rate of noma; 46% of the rapid progression, 40% knew the appropriate treatment and only 18% the associated risk factors. Participants reported having attended, between 1985 and 2025, a total of 43 potential cases in children and adults (ages 4-79), between stages 1-3. Undernutrition was the predominant comorbidity in children, while adults frequently presented with immunosuppression. Key barriers for diagnosis and treatment included limited training, misdiagnosis, weak healthcare infrastructure, delayed access to care, and cultural beliefs influencing help-seeking.
CONCLUSIONS: In Latin America, there are critical knowledge gaps on noma among frontline healthcare providers. Reported suspected cases in recent years occurred predominantly in adults, although pediatric cases were also described. These findings highlight the need for strengthened regional medical education, particularly in Spanish and Portuguese. Integration of noma-related content into existing skin-neglected tropical disease and oral health programs may improve clinical awareness and support earlier identification of suspected cases, contributing to improved clinical guidance and health policy development in the region.

articles.title: The "New" Frozen Frontier of World War II: Air War at Extreme Altitude.
articles.abstract: Cold injury was a largely overlooked medical and operational crisis in Allied aviation medicine in the early days of World War II. Although extreme cold had shaped military outcomes for centuries, the rapid ascent of fighting aircraft of this era to altitudes above 8000 m exposed aircrews to unprecedented hypobaric and thermal stress. Early in the conflict, aviation medicine lagged behind engineering advances, and frostbite reached epidemic proportions. The historical record reveals that inadequate equipment, poor training, flawed oxygen-delivery systems, and structural vulnerabilities of aircraft were primary contributors to injury. Moreover, awareness of the mechanisms of cold injury in the early 1940s, at least in the English-speaking world, was at such a basic level that the therapeutic paradigm of rapid rewarming of frostbite injury was not to be readily accepted until the following decade. Nonetheless, the findings of military medical investigators combined with political pressure from civilian consultants prompted high-level review of cold injury in aviators. This ultimately forced reforms at Wright Field, the center of US aeromedical development during the war. Solutions were implemented that included improved oxygen-mask design, protective plexiglass gun-port coverings, individualized cold-weather gear, and mandatory oxygen-use protocols. By mid-1944, frostbite incidence had markedly declined among aircrews. However, the failure to transfer these lessons to ground forces during the winter of 1944 to 1945 underscored persistent gaps in institutional learning and highlighted the need for systematic dissemination of operational medical knowledge across military branches.

articles.title: From learning to practice: A theory-informed qualitative study of why interprofessional collaboration remains difficult to enact.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Interprofessional collaboration (IPC) is essential for high-quality, integrated care, and interprofessional education (IPE) aims to prepare future health professionals for collaborative practice. However, positive educational experiences and attitudes towards teamwork do not necessarily translate into collaboration in clinical practice. A theory-informed understanding of the determinants shaping this translation is needed to better align interprofessional learning with the realities of healthcare practice. We explore the determinants of IPC among senior health professions students and recent graduates using a theory-informed qualitative approach.
METHODS: This qualitative study formed the first phase of a sequential mixed-methods project. Eight focus group discussions were conducted with 37 senior students and recent graduates from medicine, pharmacy, dental medicine, and health sciences at Qatar University. Data were analysed using a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis, with codes mapped to the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) and iteratively refined into higher-order themes.
RESULTS: Nine themes were identified across seven TDF domains, represented through six analytic groupings, with Knowledge and Skills combined for reporting. Participants generally expressed positive intentions towards collaboration, but IPC in practice was constrained by hierarchical relationships, unclear professional roles, limited opportunities to collaborate, and inconsistent reinforcement. Participants described closer collaboration in high-acuity settings, whereas hierarchical norms appeared more pronounced in lower-complexity settings. Facilitators and preceptors were perceived as influential in reinforcing or discouraging collaborative behaviour.
DISCUSSION: IPC is shaped by interacting individual, social, and environmental determinants. Although prelicensure IPE can foster readiness for collaboration, participants may struggle to enact this learning when educational preparation does not reflect practice realities. Strengthening IPC requires alignment between curriculum design, assessment, faculty development, and clinical practice environments, alongside continued interprofessional learning beyond qualification.

articles.title: Assessment of Interprofessional Trauma Team Performance and Cohesion During a Civil-Military Large-Scale Live Simulation Exercise-A Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Large-scale civil-military simulation exercises allow interprofessional trauma teams practice leadership, communication, and decision-making under high stress; however, evidence on their contribution to multinational interoperability is limited. We assessed trauma-team performance and cohesion during a multinational live simulation and identified barriers and enablers of interoperability.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospective cross-sectional observational study was conducted during NATO Vigorous Warrior 2024 across eight Role 2 hospitals in Hungary. Trauma teams (n = 75) from nine nations managed simulated major trauma casualties. Performance was evaluated using the Non-Technical Skills for Surgeons (NOTSS) and Team Emergency Assessment Measure (TEAM) frameworks. Four expert assessors made structured observations, and members completed post-scenario self-assessments; team and assessor ratings were compared descriptively.
RESULTS: Teams rated their overall performance more favorably than assessors across all domains: overall performance was rated excellent by 57% of members versus 25% of assessors, who rated 25% of teams poor or below average. Discrepancies were greatest for leadership clarity, structured communication, and role allocation. Designated leadership, clear chains of command, and organized equipment were associated with better decision-making and task completion. Multinational composition enriched problem-solving but created communication barriers, tensions, and documentation inconsistencies; absent standardized debriefing further limited structured learning.
CONCLUSIONS: Leadership clarity, structured communication, and psychological safety underpin effective multinational trauma teamwork. The perceived-observed performance gap, which may reflect self-assessment leniency and assessor stringency ("hawk-dove" effect), indicates scope for calibration through structured feedback. Standardized training frameworks, harmonized resuscitation protocols, and structured debriefing are needed to improve interoperability and readiness across civil-military trauma systems.

articles.title: Reflective seminars for the promotion of mental health in medical education: a qualitative model in a Latin American context.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medical training sustains a persistent tension between academic demands, emotional well-being, and professional identity. In Latin America, mental health promotion remains scarcely integrated into the formal curriculum. This study examined a reflective seminar consisting of a single standardised four-hour session delivered once to each of 54 groups of second-year students (20 students per group; 1,080 students in total) during the preclinical phase of medical training. The study explored participants' perceptions of the seminar's pedagogical dynamics and its perceived effects.
METHODS: Qualitative interpretive research was conducted using a hermeneutic-phenomenological design. Four focus groups were held with 26 research participants (14 students and 12 teachers) who had taken part in the seminar and provided written informed consent. Inductive-deductive thematic analysis combined open and axial coding, source triangulation, and collegial calibration to support interpretive rigour.
RESULTS: Three interrelated dimensions were identified. Perceived institutional care legitimised well-being as an academic concern. Psychological safety favoured openness, peer support, and reflective deliberation. Teachers acted as emotional facilitators and models of professional vulnerability, which participants associated with a reconfiguration of pedagogical relationships and of the hidden curriculum. Neither psychological safety nor perceived benefit was uniform: some students remained disengaged, participation was lower in one group with a more reserved facilitator, and one teacher described feeling overwhelmed when students later sought individual support.
CONCLUSION: The reflective seminar may function as a relational pedagogical infrastructure that articulates well-being and professional identity. Participants described curricular integration, a climate of trust, and teacher modelling as enabling ecological readings of distress and as displacing individualising narratives. These findings provide qualitative evidence of plausible, perceived mechanisms by which formative interventions can humanise medical education, and they generate hypotheses for comparable contexts rather than demonstrated effects.

articles.title: Surviving the glocal ecosystem: Academic dissonance, cultural adaptation, and coping among international medical students in the Caribbean.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The globalization of medical education has increased international student mobility, with many students choosing to study abroad to gain exposure to different healthcare systems and cultural environments. Despite this global trend, limited research exists on the experiences of international students attending newly established medical schools in developing regions. This study aims to explore the decision-making process, motivations, challenges, and adaptation strategies of international medical students at a brand-new medical school founded in 2023 in the Caribbean.
METHODS: A qualitative, descriptive phenomenological approach was employed to explore students' lived experiences. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 12 international students of various backgrounds and demographics. The interview questions focused on decision-making, perceived benefits, academic and cultural challenges, and coping strategies. Thematic analysis was used to identify key patterns and themes.
RESULTS: Students were primarily motivated by the ability to begin their medical education without delays, citing flexible admissions, immediate program availability, and small class sizes. Challenges included academic rigor, adjusting to the flipped classroom model, cultural differences, homesickness, limited island resources, and concerns about the school's newness. Adaptation strategies included personalized study methods, mindfulness, physical activity, social support networks, and environmental resourcefulness.
DISCUSSION: International students chose Caribbean medical schools for accessible admissions, personalized education, and career alignment despite financial, social, and reputational challenges. They faced academic, cultural, and emotional pressures but used resilience and adaptive coping, achieving partial integration and academic progress, consistent with theoretical frameworks. These findings highlight the need for a comprehensive student support programme addressing academic, cultural, emotional, logistical, and reputational needs to promote well-being, retention, and successful adaptation.

articles.title: Perceptions of mentees and mentors regarding one-to-one mentorship program at a medical college: a cross-sectional study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Mentorship is an important component of undergraduate medical education, providing academic guidance, professional development, and psychosocial support. One-to-one mentorship programmes facilitate individualized mentor-mentee relationships; however, their effectiveness depends on participant perceptions and programme implementation. This study aimed to evaluate the perceptions of mentees and mentors regarding an ongoing one-to-one mentorship program in a medical college.
METHODS: A cross-sectional mixed-methods study was conducted among undergraduate medical students enrolled in an institutional one-to-one mentorship program and faculty mentors with experience mentoring at least one batch of students within the previous five years. A total of 418 mentees and 68 mentors completed validated semi-structured questionnaires, yielding response rates of 69.7% and 94.4%, respectively. The questionnaires explored perceptions of the mentorship program - preferred mentoring methods, strengths, limitations, and suggestions for improvement. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics and Chi-square tests, while qualitative responses were analysed using thematic analysis.
RESULTS: Among mentees, 89.7% perceived that the mentorship program improved their confidence and competence, while 84.4% reported improved academic performance. Most mentees preferred being given an opportunity to choose their mentors (93.3%) and favoured mentors associated with their current phase of study or subject area (83.0%). Among mentors, 86.7% believed that mentorship enhanced students' confidence and competence, and 83.8% perceived that mentorship helped reduce student burnout. One-to-one mentoring emerged, as the most preferred mentoring model among both mentees (65.6%) and mentors (73.5%). Significant associations were observed between mentoring preferences and students' gender and phase of MBBS training, while mentors' years of teaching experience influenced perceptions regarding mentorship outcomes. Qualitative analysis identified individualized guidance, academic support, communication, emotional support, and confidence building as major strengths, whereas limited interaction frequency and variable student engagement were identified as important challenges.
CONCLUSION: Both mentees and mentors perceived the one-to-one mentorship programme positively, particularly regarding its contributions to academic development, confidence building, and student well-being. Enhancing mentor training, increasing the frequency of mentor-mentee interactions, and incorporating greater flexibility in mentor allocation and phase-specific mentoring support may further strengthen programme effectiveness and improve educational outcomes.
