articles.title: From XR-derived performance metrics to an objective performance score in point-of-care ultrasound.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) quality depends on operator proficiency. As POCUS training expands, scalable approaches to performance evaluation are needed. Current performance evaluation relies largely on examiner-intensive Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCE). Extended Reality (XR) technologies offer opportunities to capture objective performance metrics and provide the digitization needed to support automated and standardised performance evaluations. The objective of this study was to explore the use of XR-derived performance metrics and examine how an automated performance score using these metrics relates to OSCE performance.
METHODS: Medical students (novices), physicians with limited ultrasound experience (intermediates), and experienced physicians and sonographers (experts) performed a cardiac ultrasound task on a phantom, while using a phone as a probe and wearing a HoloLens that immerses them in an XR environment. They were tasked to obtain four cardiac POCUS views. OSCE was scored by two independent experts. Probe trajectories were derived from the phone and were used to extract kinematic metrics, such as time, path length, straightness index, and dimensionless squared jerk. These were complemented with image quality surrogates (position and angle deviation), and gaze behaviour (gaze shifts to the display). A metric-based performance score was constructed using multivariable regression and compared with OSCE scores.
RESULTS: Ninety participants were included (34 novices, 31 intermediates, 25 experts). The OSCE scoring demonstrated excellent inter-rater reliability (ICC 0.97) and clear discrimination across experience levels. Kinematic and gaze metrics aligned with experience level and OSCE performance, whereas image quality surrogates showed weaker associations. Factor analysis of the XR-derived performance metrics identified two underlying domains of technical performance; probe handling and image quality, with gaze behaviour emerging as a distinct construct. The automated performance score showed a moderate to good correlation with OSCE performance (ρ = 0.69). Replacing XR-derived image quality surrogates with expert-rated image quality substantially improved associations (ρ = 0.91).
CONCLUSIONS: XR-derived, automated performance scoring represents a promising, scalable approach for formative feedback and early-stage screening, particularly in novice learners, while reducing examiner burden. These findings lay the foundation for further development toward fully automated ultrasound performance tracking. Further validation is required before use in high-stakes or fully automated assessment.

articles.title: Large language models in radiology education: a systematic review of applications and learning outcomes.
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: This systematic review aimed to map how large language models (LLMs) are used in radiology education, grade their reported outcomes, and appraise evidence quality.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We searched PubMed, Europe PMC, and ERIC (November 2022-October 2026) for original studies of LLMs in the radiology education of medical students or residents, including educator-rated LLM materials intended for them. Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts independently. Studies were grouped by application, outcomes were graded with a modified Kirkpatrick framework, and quality was assessed with the Medical Education Research Study Quality Instrument (MERSQI).
RESULTS: Twenty-two studies (23 reports) were included. Twelve involved residents, five medical students, two mixed groups, and three had no learners. Applications were question generation (n = 7), feedback on learners' work (n = 6), content generation and tutoring (n = 4), simulation or personalized curricula (n = 2), and learners' own use (n = 3). LLM-generated questions matched expert questions on recall items but were weaker on clinical-reasoning items, and their apparent quality partly depended on human selection. Report feedback was moderately to highly accurate and generally welcomed. Only three studies measured learning; the rest evaluated LLM output, learner reactions, or case exposure, and none measured behavior. Mean MERSQI was 9.6 of 18 (range 6.0-12.5); 18 studies were single-center, and one was randomized.
CONCLUSION: LLMs produce usable teaching materials, but evidence that they improve learning is limited and of low to moderate quality. They should be supervised until controlled multicenter studies are available.

articles.title: Surgery Is Not a Place: Time-to-Scalpel, Surgical Throughput, and Dynamic Load Balancing in Large-Scale Combat Operations.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Modern combat casualty care emphasizes rapid evacuation to surgical capability as a proxy for timely operative intervention. In large-scale combat operations (LSCO), however, high casualty density and finite surgical throughput may delay care even after arrival. We evaluated how operative capacity and casualty routing influence time-to-scalpel (TTS) during sustained combat.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This non-human subjects study developed a Division-scale discrete-event simulation representing an 18,000-person force, 9 evacuation origins, three Role 2 facilities each containing a full forward resuscitative and surgical detachment (FRSD) with two operating tables, and one Role 3 facility with four operating tables. The campaign lasted 36 days, with individual 30-day mortality follow-up. Eight casualty densities ranged from 1 to 15 combat casualties per 1,000 personnel per day. Four routing tactics were evaluated: Primary, Alternate, Bypass, and Smart, which prioritized surgical access for the highest-acuity patients. Mean TTS was the primary outcome; mean, median, and 95th-percentile TTS were conditional on operative start. Other outcomes included access among all surgical candidates and combat 30-day case fatality rate (CFR). Routing comparisons used 20 seed-matched replications per scenario with Holm adjustment. Bypass sensitivity analyses at densities 3, 9, and 15 varied delay-related mortality penalties by ±20% and replaced each FRSD with one forward resuscitative and surgical squad (FRSS).
RESULTS: The main experiment included 920 replications across 32 scenarios. At density 15, mean TTS was 136.24 hours with Primary, 19.24 with Bypass, and 82.53 with Smart. Both bypass-capable tactics reduced mean TTS relative to Primary at densities 7-15 (adjusted P < .05). Under Primary, the mean fraction of preoperative delay attributable to surgical queueing exceeded 50% at density 9. Compared with Bypass, Smart shortened urgent-cohort TTS at all tested densities but lengthened TTS among the remaining surgical patients at densities 5-15 (all adjusted P < .05). Smart also had higher CFR at density 9 (+0.307 percentage points; adjusted P = .016) but lower CFR at density 15 (-0.544 percentage points; adjusted P = .010). FRSSs increased TTS and CFR at all 3 sensitivity densities (all adjusted P < .05). Substantial surgical delays persisted under both mortality-penalty assumptions.
CONCLUSIONS: Under the modeled LSCO conditions, operative congestion increasingly drove delay to surgery. Load balancing casualty routing tactics may preserve operative access more effectively than fixed proximity-based routing alone. However, prioritizing surgical access for the highest-acuity patients does not uniformly improve access or mortality across the casualty population.

articles.title: Learning through Caregiving: A Qualitative Study of Reflections From a Medical Student Elective for New Parents.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Many new parents in medicine, particularly medical students, do not feel supported by their institutions. One structural support present in most pediatric residencies is a new parent elective; however this is rarely available for students. This study seeks to better understand the lived experience of medical students during a new parent/caregiving elective at the University of Minnesota to learn how we can better support student parents.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective qualitative study of students' written reflections during a caregiving elective, using reflexive thematic analysis through an inductive approach to identify common patterns and ideas within the dataset.
RESULTS: We analyzed 54 reflections from 16 students (39% of invited participants (n=41)). We found three themes: 1) Students' experiences of the common challenges of early parenthood prompts or leads to personal transformation; 2) Students rely on relationships from inside and outside of medicine to find support and community; and 3) The intersections of parenthood, patienthood, and medical training influence how students interact with the medical system and contribute to their identities as future physicians. As students experienced parenting, they often related these experiences to their medical training in ways that likely affect their growing identities as future physicians.
CONCLUSIONS: Student parents who participated in this caregiving elective described common experiences of becoming a parent and utilized these experiences to develop skills that will help them become better doctors. They also appreciated support from this elective. Additional institutional support may better facilitate their emerging parent and physician identities.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence hallucinations in large language models for medical education and healthcare: a scoping review of detection, mitigation, and governance.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in medical education and healthcare. Yet AI hallucinations-plausible but inaccurate, unsupported, or fabricated information or citations-may compromise educational integrity, clinical judgment, patient safety, and trust. This scoping review mapped evidence on their nature, detection and validation, mitigation, and educational and governance implications.
METHODS: This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and informed by the Arksey and O'Malley framework. Reporting followed the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science were systematically searched for English-language sources published from January 1, 2018, to July 31, 2026. Study selection and data extraction were independently performed by two reviewers. Findings were synthesized using descriptive thematic analysis.
RESULTS: Of 2,051 identified records, 21 sources were included in the final synthesis after duplicate removal and screening. These included five empirical or model-evaluation studies and 16 review, conceptual, or opinion-based sources. The analysis identified five main themes and 13 subthemes: (1) conceptualization and manifestations of AI hallucinations in healthcare; (2) detection, assessment, and validation of hallucinations; (3) mitigation strategies for improving the reliability of generative AI outputs; (4) educational implications and critical AI literacy; and (5) governance, accountability, and trustworthy implementation in healthcare. Retrieval-augmented generation, structured prompt design, output-verification methods, and human oversight were among the most frequently identified approaches for reducing hallucination-related risks.
CONCLUSION: AI hallucinations are not merely technical errors; they represent a multidimensional challenge to the safe and responsible use of LLMs in medical education and healthcare. Reducing their risks requires a multilayered approach that includes evidence-based validation, human oversight, critical AI literacy, redesign of educational assessment, and transparent governance and accountability frameworks.

articles.title: Conference on Medical Education and Research Writings during Arbaeen at College of Medicine, University Warith Al-Anbiyaa, and University of Karbala 22-23 and 26 July 2026.
articles.journal: JPMA. The Journal of the Pakistan Medical Association
articles.abstract: An academic programme spanning three days took place in Karbala, Iraq on 22-23 and 26 July 2026, linking medical education and training in scientific writing to the service orientation of the Arbaeen pilgrimage. Workshops held at the College of Medicine, University of Warith Al-Anbiyaa and at the College of Medicine, University of Kerbala brought together Iraqi and Pakistani educators and clinicians to discuss responsible artificial intelligence, qualitative research, scientific writing, curriculum integration, regenerative medicine, precision geriatric care, radiology, surgery, and disaster management. Practical workshops enabled participants to move away from information transfer to application. A critical synthesis revealed four interlinked themes: service and scholarship as an integrated continuum; learning by doing; responsible innovation; and academic solidarity across borders. The programme provided a forum for future mentorship and collaboration in research but future events will need to include prospective evaluation and follow-up of the results of the academic activities. These areas can shape the planning and evaluation of future conferences.

articles.title: Mentor and mentee experiences of the NMC-CBME mentorship programme in India: a two-centre qualitative study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: India's National Medical Commission mandated a formal mentorship programme within competency-based medical education for all MBBS students. However, evidence regarding how mentors and mentees experience this programme remains limited. This study explored the perceptions and experiences of both groups across two geographically and demographically distinct tertiary-care institutions.
METHODS: A two-centre parallel qualitative study was conducted at Site A (Jharkhand) and Site B (Arunachal Pradesh). Mentee perspectives were collected through eight focus group discussions (four/site) with MBBS students. Mentor perspectives were explored through in-depth interviews (15 at Site A & 24 at Site B). Focus Group Discussion (FGD) data were analysed using inductive thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke), while In Depth Interviews (IDI) data were analysed using framework analysis. Site-level analyses were conducted independently and integrated through cross-site thematic comparison. Reporting followed COREQ guidelines.
RESULTS: 39 mentors and 56 mentees participated. Nine thematic domains emerged. Eight were convergent across both sites: structural and implementation inadequacies; scheduling deficiencies and boundary violations; differential academic support quality; psychosocial support potential constrained by structural barriers; mentor unpreparedness and quality variability; hierarchical communication barriers; phase-specific mentorship needs; and an accountability vacuum with absent feedback mechanisms. One theme (cultural and contextual specificity) was unique to Site B. Across all data sources, participants endorsed mentorship in principle but described implementation as structurally inadequate. Informal communication channels and social interactions, organically adopted at Site B, appeared to mitigate some gaps that participants at Site A identified as desired improvements.
CONCLUSIONS: This study concludes that the convergence of findings across two sites suggests that these implementation challenges may reflect broader features of the programme; however, this interpretation should be considered an analytical inference requiring confirmation in broader settings. Strengthening mentorship requires protected time, structured mentor training, explicit confidentiality safeguards, separation of mentoring from summative evaluation, and institutional recognition. Findings further indicate that context-sensitive adaptation is essential, particularly for minority and tribal student populations.

articles.title: Evaluating an AI-Powered Patient Simulator for Communication Skills Training: One-Year Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Clinical communication skills are a core yet complex competency in medical education and practice. However, early-stage medical students often struggle to apply communication frameworks in practice due to limited opportunities for structured simulation training. Generative AI (GenAI)-supported training has the potential to offer a scalable and innovative approach for clinical communication skills training.
OBJECTIVE: This study examined the longitudinal development of medical students' clinical communication skills over 1 academic year and investigated whether AI-powered simulation contributed to differential improvement relative to conventional training. In addition, the study explored motivational, behavioral, and affective mechanisms associated with communication skills development.
METHODS: A nonblinded randomized controlled design was used at a medical school in the United Kingdom, with students assigned either to the control group (n=28, 56%) or to the AI group (n=22, 44%), who practiced with SimPatient, a patient-simulator chatbot accessed through a web browser. Communication skills performance was assessed using standardized objective structured clinical examinations (OSCE) scores relative to the pass marks to enable comparison across time points. Paired t tests and difference-in-differences (DID) analyses were conducted between groups and over time to examine changes in communication skills. Latent change score modeling was used to identify predictors of communication skills change. Sentiment analysis was conducted on 6120 comments from AI-student conversations. Finally, a system quality survey was used to assess participants' feedback on the AI-powered simulator.
RESULTS: Latent change score modeling showed that gains in intrinsic motivation and behavioral learning were significant predictors of students' communication skills change. The AI group showed a greater descriptive increase in communication skills than the control group, yet the between-group difference was not statistically significant. Within the AI group, consultations whose lexical tone trended more strongly toward resolution (consultation tone) were descriptively associated with communication skills improvement; given the small subsample (n=17), this finding is reported as exploratory. The AI group's confidence level in AI use was negatively associated with communication skills improvement, while the group nevertheless reported a generally high level of satisfaction with the system.
CONCLUSIONS: In this study, medical students' clinical communication skills increased over the academic year, with this development most strongly associated with their motivation and behavioral engagement; the AI-supported group did not differ significantly from conventional training. The simulator responded appropriately and provided a usable environment for practicing foundational communication behaviors but was limited in capturing the affective complexity, vulnerability, and narrative unpredictability of real clinical encounters. In conclusion, this study suggests that GenAI holds promise for supporting foundational clinical communication training and providing positive practice environments, thereby fostering motivation and behavioral engagement.

articles.title: Regulation and Ethical Frameworks for AI in Health Professions Education: A Critical Narrative Review.
articles.journal: Journal of advances in medical education & professionalism
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Integrating artificial intelligence (AI)-particularly generative AI and large language models (LLMs)-into health professions education offers substantial pedagogical opportunities, while highlighting critical gaps in existing ethical and regulatory frameworks. This critical narrative review examines how contemporary literature conceptualizes and addresses these challenges.
METHODS: Publications from 2020-2025 were identified through searching PubMed, Scopus, and ERIC, focusing on AI, medical and health professions education, ethics, governance, and regulation. The initial search yielded 452 records; following two-stage screening (title/abstract and full-text review), thirty-four sources met the pre-defined inclusion criteria. These sources, including empirical studies, systematic reviews, policy documents, and conceptual papers, were included. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to synthesize the findings, while SANRA (Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles) informed the weighting of sources, which were categorized into high-, moderate-, and low-weight tiers.
RESULTS: Four themes emerged: 1) a regulatory vacuum marked by policy lag and fragmented institutional responses; 2) reinterpretation of autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice in relation to opaque, datadriven systems, 3) generative AI's impact on scholarship, authorship, and academic integrity; and 4) equity, bias, and professional identity formation in AImediated learning environments. Integrating these themes with crosssector frameworks and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the review develops a riskbased governance taxonomy for AI in Health Professions Education, distinguishing low, medium and highrisk educational use cases.
CONCLUSION: This synthesis indicates that current literature favors evolving beyond reactive policies. Consequently, we propose a theoretical shift toward risk-proportionate governance. We suggest that human-in-the-loop pedagogy should be prioritized as a conceptual framework to guide future research and policy development, rather than presenting it as a validated outcome.

articles.title: Gradual Transformation toward Expertise: A Grounded Theory of Clinical Medical Teachers' Development Process.
articles.journal: Journal of advances in medical education & professionalism
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Expertise is an experiential capability that cannot be acquired through formal education alone; rather, it develops through sustained reflection and iterative practice. Despite the importance of expert clinical faculty, the process of attaining this educational expertise has not been systematically conceptualized. This study was conducted to develop a paradigmatic model of the educational competency development process in clinical medical faculty and identify its dimensions, components, and interrelationships.
METHODS: This qualitative grounded theory study was conducted in 2024-2025 at Iran University of Medical Sciences using the Corbin and Strauss approach (2015). A total of 15 participants, including 13 clinical faculty members (with at least five years of teaching experience and recognized teaching competence) and 2 medical students, were initially recruited through purposive sampling. Snowball sampling was used solely as a recruitment technique to identify additional information-rich participants. As we collected and analyzed data, we used theoretical sampling. This helped us refine the categories and reach theoretical saturation. Data were collected through semi_structured, in-depth interviews lasting 30-50 minutes (mean: 45 minutes). All interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Data were analyzed concurrently with data collection using the constant comparative method, including open coding, category development, contextual analysis, and theoretical integration. Rigor was ensured through prolonged engagement with the data, member checking, peer debriefing, and the maintenance of an audit trail.
RESULTS: Data analysis led to the emergence of the core category, "Gradual Transformation toward Expertise," which explains how clinical faculty members evolve from expert clinicians into transformative educators. This process is dynamic, non-linear, and highly context-dependent. Five interrelated themes describe this developmental trajectory: 1) reflection and competence development, 2) experiential learning and clinical observation, 3) mentorship and knowledge transfer, 4) motivational and contextual influences, and 5) barriers and professional transformation. The process was shaped by six contextual factors: a) the complex and dynamic nature of clinical education; b) the need for continuous competency development; c) generational differences in teaching and learning styles; d) workload and competing clinical responsibilities; e) the necessity of integrating practical experience with scientific evidence; and f) an organizational culture that prioritizes treatment over education. Additionally, causal conditions such as multiple professional pressures and generational gaps further influenced the pace and direction of this transformation. Overall, the findings depict expertise development as a gradual, evolving process through which faculty members reconcile their clinical and educational roles to become effective and transformative clinical educators.
CONCLUSION: Clinical teacher expertise develops through a dynamic interplay of individual effort, experiential learning, and environmental factors. This transformation requires personal commitment to lifelong learning and reflection, supported by organizational initiatives such as faculty development programs, mentoring, and aligned incentive systems. The proposed grounded theory provides a practical framework for designing professional development initiatives and fostering educational settings that enhance expertise in similar non-Western contexts.

articles.title: Dual-edged swords: a qualitative study of protective and risk factors shaping mental health among Chinese health professions students.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Mental health challenges among health professions students are a global concern, yet how these challenges manifest within socio-cultural contexts like China remains underexplored. This study utilised Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory to investigate the risk and protective factors influencing the mental health of health professions students in China.
METHODS: This qualitative study employed reflexive thematic analysis to examine the experiences and perspectives of 30 undergraduates from clinical medicine, nursing, pharmacy, and allied health programmes. Participants were selected by purposive sampling and data were collected using semi-structured individual in-depth interviews.
RESULTS: During the data analysis, five interconnected themes were identified. Within each theme, participants described factors operating as risks, as protective resources, or as dual-edged forces depending on context. The themes are: (1) Academic Pressure and Interpersonal Dynamics within Immediate Environments (Microsystem); (2) Fragmentation and Dysfunction within Support Networks (Mesosystem); (3) Institutional Logics and Structural Constraints (Exosystem); (4) The Internalisation of Macro-Cultural Values and Behavioural Guidance (Macrosystem); and (5) Chronological Interactions and the Reshaping of Developmental Trajectories (Chronosystem).
CONCLUSIONS: The findings reveal a complex transaction across all ecological levels, highlighting that student mental health is predominantly shaped by systemic and cultural forces beyond the individual. This study provides a foundational ecological model for understanding these challenges and suggests that future research quantitatively examine the interactions between these themes, compare experiences across different health disciplines, and evaluate the effectiveness of support interventions tailored to specific ecological levels.

articles.title: From fragmentation to integration: rethinking nutrition education in undergraduate medical curriculum in Pakistan through a mixed-methods study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nutrition plays a central role in the prevention and management of both communicable and noncommunicable diseases, yet its integration within undergraduate medical education remains inconsistent. This study aimed to assess the current status of nutrition education in MBBS programs in Pakistan and to propose a structured framework for curriculum enhancement.
METHODS: A mixed methods study was conducted in Rawalpindi and Islamabad, Pakistan. The study included a structured review of the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council MBBS curriculum 2024, a cross-sectional survey of 242 final-year medical students from four medical colleges, and in-depth interviews with 13 faculty members across key disciplines. The sample size for the quantitative component was calculated using OpenEpi, based on a population of 650 students. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and a semi-structured interview guide. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while qualitative data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings from all components were triangulated.
RESULTS: The curriculum review demonstrated that nutrition content is present but remains fragmented, with limited clinical integration and lack of defined competencies. Among students, 88.4 percent recognized the importance of nutrition in medical education, while only 28.1 percent perceived the curriculum as adequate. Exposure to nutrition was highest in community medicine (80.2 percent) and biochemistry (53.7 percent), but substantially lower in clinical disciplines such as internal medicine (28.9 percent) and pediatrics (36.4 percent). Teaching was predominantly lecture-based (78.5 percent), with limited use of interactive methods. Students reported moderate confidence in general nutrition knowledge but low preparedness for managing nutrition-related conditions. Qualitative findings highlighted gaps in integration, assessment, and clinical application, along with a need for structured curriculum reform.
CONCLUSION: Despite recent curricular advancements, nutrition education in undergraduate medical training remains insufficiently integrated and clinically oriented. The proposed competency-based framework offers a practical approach to strengthening nutrition education within existing curricular structures, with the potential to improve clinical preparedness and align medical training with population health needs.

articles.title: How does creative enquiry enable us to deal with uncertainty?
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Uncertainty is an inherent and pervasive feature of medical practice. Here, uncertainty refers to the subjective perception and affective experience encountered by medical students and clinicians. Difficulties in managing uncertainty are associated with impaired communication in shared decision-making and may contribute to clinical burnout. Despite longstanding recognition of its importance, including recent UK curricular reforms focused on "managing uncertainty," it remains insufficiently addressed in medical practice. This study seeks to address this gap by examining how creative enquiry may support both learners and clinicians in engaging with uncertainty in practice.
METHODS: We undertook a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with ten participants (five medical students; five clinicians, comprising four general practitioners and one infectious disease specialist) with prior experience of creative enquiry. Participants were recruited through convenience sampling from a creative-enquiry student-selected component (SSC) and clinician networks. Interviews were conducted online, audio-recorded, and transcribed verbatim. Data were analysed inductively using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis, supported by NVivo 14. Student participants had completed the SSC in preclinical years and were interviewed during clinical training. Creative enquiry activities included engagement with patient-generated creative work, arts-based practices (e.g. photography, collage, creative writing, sculpture), and facilitated group dialogue.
RESULTS: Three analytically related dimensions were generated: Issues, Processes, and Effects. Participants described uncertainty as intensified by binary epistemic cultures and the marginalisation of emotional experience. Creative enquiry involved engagement with indeterminate processes characterised by the absence of singular correct outcomes and the unpredictability of creative production. These processes enabled emotional processing, supporting participants to "digest" affective responses, and fostered a stance of "permission to play," legitimising experimentation and imperfection. Repeated engagement contributed to the normalisation of uncertainty, with parallels drawn to exposure. Reported effects included restoration of voice and recognition, reduction in the emotional burden of uncertainty, and enhanced reflexivity. Participants described an expanded capacity for perspective-taking and more complex conceptualisations of practice ("seeing medicine in three dimensions").
CONCLUSIONS: This study extends current understandings of uncertainty in medical education by identifying creative enquiry as a practice that integrates epistemic and affective engagement. We propose a Personal, Protective, and Embracing (PPE) framework, through which creative enquiry supports (i) articulation and emotional processing (Personal), (ii) containment and respite (Protective), and (iii) acceptance and constructive engagement with uncertainty (Embracing). These findings contribute to the operationalisation of "managing uncertainty" as a curricular competency and support further theoretically informed and empirical investigation of creative pedagogies in medical education.

articles.title: Integrating nutrition counseling into clinical skills training: a simulation-based interprofessional education program for medical and nursing students.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The increasing prevalence of diet-related chronic diseases highlights the urgent need for effective nutrition education in health professions training. This study evaluated a simulation-based interprofessional education (IPE) program designed to enhance nutrition counseling knowledge and self-efficacy among medical and nursing students.
METHODS: A multimethod study was conducted with 89 medical and nursing students. Participants were recruited through university announcements and class meetings. Participation was voluntary and did not affect grades. No financial incentives were offered. Participants completed a 4-week program consisting of: (1) online nutrition modules, (2) interprofessional team-based learning sessions, and (3) standardized patient simulations. Quantitative measures included pre- and post-intervention assessments of nutrition knowledge, counseling self-efficacy, and interprofessional attitudes. Effect sizes (Cohen's d) were calculated for all comparisons. Qualitative data were collected through six focus groups with a purposive subsample of 24 participants and analyzed using inductive thematic analysis until saturation was reached.
RESULTS: Participants demonstrated significant improvements in nutrition knowledge (mean difference: 2.39, 95% CI [1.69, 3.10], Cohen's d = 0.73, p < 0.001) and counseling self-efficacy (mean difference: 16.52, 95% CI [14.99, 18.05], Cohen's d = 2.31, p < 0.001). Interprofessional attitudes also showed positive changes, particularly in teamwork and collaboration domains. Qualitative analysis revealed three main themes: (1) increased confidence in nutrition counseling, (2) appreciation for interprofessional perspectives, and (3) recognition of nutrition's role in comprehensive patient care. Participants valued the simulation component as particularly effective for skill development.
CONCLUSIONS: Participation in this simulation-based interprofessional education program was associated with short-term improvements in nutrition counseling knowledge and self-efficacy among health professions students. The integration of online learning, team-based activities, and standardized patient encounters provides a comprehensive approach to nutrition education. These findings offer preliminary evidence that this model may help address the gap in clinical nutrition training. Further research with controlled designs and longer follow-up is warranted.

articles.title: Comparison of AI and Manual Coding of Medical Students' Reflections: An Asynchronous Discussion Board Exploration.
articles.journal: WMJ : official publication of the State Medical Society of Wisconsin
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) for medical education research remains controversial. Although AI has the potential to revolutionize qualitative research analysis, concerns regarding its validity and accuracy remain barriers to its use in research. We sought to compare AI-generated qualitative coding with human coding.
METHODS: As part of a mandatory course, third-year medical students watched 2 health care-related videos and responded to prompts on a virtual discussion board. Students' posts were anonymized. Human coders met multiple times over a 4-month period to create a code list, generate themes, and produce an explanatory model. Generative AI also was asked to identify the main themes. Three external reviewers with expertise in qualitative research compared each pair of human-coded and AI-generated themes.
RESULTS: Human coders required nine 60-minute meetings to code students' posts, whereas AI completed the analysis in approximately 30 seconds. Consensus among the external reviewers was that the pairs of themes were not the same or similar.
CONCLUSIONS: AI required substantially less time and effort than human coders. Although most reviewers concluded that AI-generated themes were not comparable to human-generated themes, this finding was not unanimous. Generative AI may facilitate and accelerate qualitative research in medical education; however, concerns regarding the validity and contextual interpretation of AI-generated analyses must be addressed before its widespread use in qualitative medical education research.

articles.title: From theory to therapy: the development of therapy scripts in medical students.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Therapeutic reasoning is a complex process prone to errors, particularly among junior doctors under time pressure. While experienced clinicians often rely on Type 1 (intuitive) thinking via therapy scripts, little is known about how these scripts develop during medical training. Insight into how therapy scripts develop and evolve could inform Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics (CPT) education and improve the safety of early-career prescribing.
METHODS: We carried out a qualitative think-aloud study with 15 medical students from years 2, 4, and 6. Students completed a diabetes case while verbalizing their reasoning, and then created a concept map and reflective questions. Transcripts were analysed using abductive thematic analysis, guided by Cook's therapy script framework and knowledge encapsulation theory. Concept maps were evaluated for structural complexity and richness of reasoning. Results were compared across the three groups of students, to investigate differences in therapy script development.
RESULTS: Therapy script development progressed from fragmented, mechanism-focused reasoning in second-year students to integrated, patient-centred reasoning in sixth-year students. Fourth-year students combined both forms of reasoning. Concept maps revealed that structural complexity and higher-level explanatory connections increased with training.
CONCLUSION: Therapy scripts develop gradually, with increasing integration and contextual sensitivity, during undergraduate medical training. Concept mapping supports reflection and reveals gaps in knowledge, complementing traditional teaching methods. Educational strategies that promote early, structured, and reflective reasoning may accelerate therapy script formation, improve metacognitive awareness, and reduce the gap between undergraduate training and safe, effective prescribing in clinical practice.

articles.title: Simulating Science Communication for Vulnerable Populations: A Project-Based Learning Exercise in Undergraduate Medical Microbiology.
articles.abstract: While undergraduate medical education relies heavily on traditional lectures to deliver foundational biomedical sciences, standard models frequently isolate pathogens and mechanisms from the socio-economic realities of healthcare and community communication. To address this gap, we implemented and evaluated a project-based active learning intervention conducted in a classroom setting in a Medical Microbiology course, challenging students to synthesize complex scientific literature and design educational brochures tailored for socially vulnerable populations. At the end of the academic semester, student perceptions were evaluated through an anonymous mixed-methods survey completed by 51 participants. The quantitative outcomes revealed high student satisfaction, with participants perceiving the instructions as highly transparent and the cognitive challenge as well-balanced. Notably, most of the students reported that the project successfully consolidated core microbiological content, while also stating that focusing on vulnerable communities significantly expanded their understanding of how social determinants impact infectious diseases. This strong positive feedback was also present in the thematic analysis of the open-ended responses, which showed that students highly valued practicing the translation of technical medical jargon into accessible, community-friendly language within this simulated exercise, which was conducted among peers and instructors. The primary challenges reported were operational, centered on group coordination and managing the heavy academic workload typical of the end of the semester. Overall, our findings suggest that integrating brochure design and public health context into the basic science curriculum effectively anchors microbiology to clinical and humanistic realities, fostering preliminary communication skills, teamwork, and social responsibility better than standard expository lessons.

articles.title: Communication Skills Training Using Simulation for Integrating Adverse Childhood Experiences into Adult Primary Care Visits for Students.
articles.journal: MedEdPORTAL : the journal of teaching and learning resources
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) can affect health and well-being throughout the lifespan. Trauma-informed care (TIC) integrates trauma understanding and resists retraumatization through fostering a safe and healing environment. This 3-hour workshop taught trainees competency-based TIC skills to identify potential signs of ACEs and other trauma in their adult patients and sensitively incorporate the impact of these experiences into their care.
METHODS: After completing prereadings, third-year medical students (MS3) and second-year physician assistant students (PA2) attended a lecture about TIC and observed a demonstration of a patient interaction. Students then completed a simulated longitudinal outpatient visit with a simulated patient (SP). The four cases of adult primary care patients presented with (1) depression and knee pain, (2) medically unexplained symptoms, (3) chronic back pain, and (4) substance use issues resulting in chronic disease. No SPs initially disclosed trauma, but all had significant ACEs. A faculty member observed the simulation, giving immediate feedback on performance. Workshops were evaluated by students in pre- and postsurveys measuring self-assessed knowledge about TIC, confidence applying TIC principles, and perceived importance of TIC.
RESULTS: One hundred and sixty-seven students completed this training, with 92 completing both pre- and postsurveys. T-test analyses indicated significant improvements across self-reported knowledge, importance, and confidence following the training, with the largest increase in confidence in trauma inquiry (+1.06 on a 1-4 scale).
DISCUSSION: This simulation training enhanced students' understanding of ACEs' influence on adult health outcomes and strengthened perceived ability to apply TIC principles, including incorporating trauma inquiry into longitudinal care.

articles.title: Ethical aspects of triage in civil and military contexts: a qualitative research of physicians' attitudes and knowledge regarding ethics in triage scenarios in.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Triage in the medical context is a screening procedure used to determine resource distribution in situations of severe restriction of medical resources. Originally, triage was designed as a method to ascertain the treatment priority of wounded soldiers on battlefields. However, ethical discussions about clinical triage were raised during the COVID-19 pandemic. In the focus stood prioritization of care in situation of limited resources.
OBJECTIVE: The purpose of our investigation was comparison of experiences and ethical attitudes towards triage among military and civil physicians. To date, there is no research available on this topic.
METHODS: We conducted 26 semi-structured, qualitative, exploratory interviews among military and civilian physicians in Germany. All the interviews were digitally audio-recorded, transcribed and anonymized. We analyzed the transcripts via the structured qualitative content analysis method.
RESULTS: Triage scenarios bring distinctive ethical challenges for the attending physicians. Military and civil physicians share a similar approach to solve the ethical conflicts arousing in such situations. Triage situation does not allow for an individual medical gold standard in the treatment of patients; therefore, the principles of autonomy, beneficence and nonmaleficence should be subordinated to the principle of social justice. Because of restriction of the patient's autonomy, the final decision-making authority lies with medical professionals. Pre-clinical triage conditions also restrict patient-physician relationship.
CONCLUSION: The ethical justification of triage follows the imperatives of life-preservation and maximization of the number of survivors. According to interviewed physicians, in both pre-clinical and clinical triage situations, medical decisions should aim rather at maximizing the well-being of the collective - whether of wounded or of a society - than at maximizing the well-being of an individual patient. Restriction of patient autonomy regarding treatment discontinuation - ex-post triage - is unavoidable in a pandemic situation.

articles.title: Mapping Complexity Lenses in Interprofessional Education and Collaborative Practice: A Scoping Review.
articles.journal: Advances in medical education and practice
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Complexity theory is increasingly applied in interprofessional education and collaborative practice (IPECP). Yet it is often unclear what researchers mean by "complexity", where it is positioned in the research process, how it informs design, analysis or interpretation, and what claims can reasonably be made from the evidence presented. This scoping review mapped how empirical IPECP studies use explicit-complexity lenses and synthesized the evidence into a moves-mechanisms-outcomes typology.
METHODS: A scoping review was conducted using JBI guidance and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. Peer-reviewed empirical IPECP studies were included if they specified an explicit-complexity lens and substantively operationalized complexity concepts in relation to IPECP. Data were charted and analyzed using descriptive counts and thematic analysis, then synthesized into a moves-mechanisms-outcomes typology.
RESULTS: Seventeen studies published between 2016 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria, with 10 published in 2023 or later. Complexity was most often positioned in conceptual framing and interpretation, with less consistent use as an analytic framework. Complexity-informed tools and resources were the most common move type (9/17), followed by system-level curriculum or micro-curriculum design (5/17). Across move types, adaptation/feedback, interdependence/networks, boundary dynamics and sensemaking/uncertainty formed the core mechanism set. Reported outcomes clustered at program/curriculum, team and student levels, with fewer studies reporting broader organizational or system-level change.
CONCLUSION: Complexity was used more consistently to frame and interpret IPECP than to provide evidence of organizational or system-level change over time. The resulting moves-mechanisms-outcomes typology offers a flexible scaffold for making the links between complexity-informed activities, change processes and reported outcomes more explicit.

articles.title: Beyond Successful Training: First Battlefield Use of Tactical Combat Casualty Care for All Service Members by Mobilized Personnel.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tactical Combat Casualty Care for All Service Members (TCCC-ASM) aims to prepare military personnel to provide self-aid and buddy aid in combat. However, the extent to which acquired TCCC-ASM skills are personally applied during real combat remains poorly understood. This study evaluated the influence of first combat experience on the practical application of TCCC-ASM among mobilized personnel during the Russo-Ukrainian War.
METHODS: A multicohort observational study was conducted between August 2022 and May 2026. Data from 5 independent cohorts were integrated, including educational assessments, structured surveys, operational observations, medical evacuation records, and rehabilitation data. The primary endpoint was the reported or directly observed application of TCCC-ASM skills in identified TCCC-relevant combat situations. Personal application of acquired TCCC-ASM skills was quantified using the Training-to-Performance Index (TP-index), a descriptive measure developed specifically for this study.
RESULTS: A total of 1,961 participants were included. Although all participants successfully completed TCCC-ASM training, 539 of 1,082 service members with combat experience (50%) contributed 1 identified index TCCC-relevant combat situation. Among 327 wounded personnel, self-aid was performed by 71 individuals (22%), whereas in the remaining 78%, the corresponding interventions were performed by other personnel through buddy aid. The TP-index was 71/539 (0.13; 95% confidence interval, 0.10-0.16), indicating limited personal application of acquired TCCC-ASM skills across identified TCCC-relevant combat situations. Major barriers to self-aid included severe pain, inability to recall procedures, panic reactions, and limited visibility; prolonged evacuation was also frequently encountered. First combat experience was associated with reassessment of training relevance and increased perceived need for refresher training.
CONCLUSIONS: A measurable gap exists between successful completion of TCCC-ASM training and personal application of acquired skills in combat. This phenomenon, defined as the Training-to-Performance Gap, highlights the limitations of relying solely on educational outcomes when evaluating military medical training. The proposed TP-index provides a descriptive measure of personal application of acquired TCCC-ASM skills in combat and, together with the observed Training-to-Performance Gap, supports consideration of refresher training following first combat experience.

articles.title: From theory to practice: a "Clarify-Bridge-Practice" seminar model for graduate medical trainees entering cardiovascular research.
articles.abstract: Graduate students in clinical medicine often possess advanced theoretical knowledge but struggle to translate it into testable hypotheses and feasible experimental designs-a "knowing-doing" gap particularly pronounced in cardiovascular physiology. To address this, we developed and evaluated a "Clarify-Bridge-Practice" (CBP) seminar model in a cardiovascular course with 87 graduate students across three cohorts (2023-2025). The intervention comprised three 80-minute seminars embedded within a 12-week course, covering: (1) causal inference and bias control, (2) critical literature synthesis, and (3) hypothesis-driven experimental design. Each seminar followed a three-phase structure: Clarify (15-minute case-driven lecture distilling core concepts), Bridge (20-minute structured scaffolding tools externalizing research reasoning), and Practice (45-minute team-based application to realistic cardiovascular cases, culminating in a mock grant defense). Outcomes were assessed via a research literacy scale, core knowledge test, rubric-scored proposals, and thematic analysis of interviews. Research literacy scores increased from 58.7 (SD = 9.3) to 78.5 (SD = 7.0) (P < 0.001); knowledge test accuracy rose from 51.8% (SD = 12.9%) to 84.5% (SD = 9.2%) (P < 0.001). Rubric scores (max 5) ranged from 3.8 (feasibility) to 4.5 (writing quality). Qualitative data indicated that scaffolding tools reduced cognitive load, while peer critique and mock defenses fostered deeper reasoning and a shift toward a researcher identity. The CBP model appears to bridge the knowing-doing gap for graduate students entering cardiovascular research, offering a structured, replicable pedagogy applicable to other clinical and translational science training contexts.

articles.title: Junior Doctors' Perceptions of Critical Care Education in Medical School and the Association with Confidence in Core Clinical Skills: A Survey of Graduates in Queensland, Australia.
articles.abstract: Confidence in critical care skills is essential for junior doctors. However, exposure to anaesthetics and critical care during medical school remains limited. This study evaluates how perceptions of undergraduate critical care teaching influence junior doctors' confidence in core clinical skills. A cross-sectional survey was distributed to junior doctors across Queensland, Australia. Quantitative data captured exposure to anaesthetics, perceived quality of teaching, and confidence in skills such as bag-mask ventilation (BMV) and pre-anaesthetic assessment. Qualitative data explored factors influencing career interest in critical care. Quantitative analysis was performed using chi-square testing, and qualitative responses underwent thematic analysis. Sixty junior doctors completed the survey. Most reported 0-2 weeks of anaesthetic placement, and 48.3% rated their teaching as "intermediate." Despite limited exposure, 61.7% reported confidence performing BMV, and 50% in pre-anaesthetic assessments. Higher perceived quality of teaching was significantly associated with greater confidence in BMV (p = 0.009) and pre-anaesthetic assessment (p = 0.008). Placement duration alone did not correlate with BMV confidence but did correlate with pre-anaesthetic assessment confidence (p = 0.004). Qualitative analysis identified themes relating to lifestyle, shift work, speciality exposure and competing interests in other specialties. l Perceived quality of undergraduate critical care education was associated with increased confidence in core skills. Placement duration alone may not improve confidence in high-risk procedures such as BMV. Implementing standardised learning objectives, structured placements, and earlier clinical exposure may improve preparedness, support safer clinical practice, and better inform career choices among junior doctors.

articles.title: Localized Debriefing Assessment for Simulation in Healthcare (DASH): Medical Student Engagement and Debriefing Assessment Validity.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Debriefing is an essential component of simulation-based education; the Debriefing Assessment for Simulation in Healthcare (DASH) is a behaviorally-anchored rating scale that evaluates debriefing quality within 6 elements. DASH was validated with trained raters evaluating simulation debriefings; the student version (DASH-SV) has not been validated. Reported DASH-SV scores cluster on the high end of the 7-point rating scale and may not accurately reflect debriefing quality. We modified the DASH-SV with localized instructions to improve student understanding and rating accuracy. We hypothesize that the localized version (DASH-LSV) will lower score inflation, yielding more accurate scores and useful feedback for simulation faculty development. Medical students at the University of Hawaii were sorted into two balanced groups. After participating in routine faculty-facilitated simulation scenarios/debriefings, group DASH-SV completed the original student version and group DASH-LSV completed the localized version. These anonymous evaluations were completed via an online survey embedded in the standard post-course feedback form. Surveys included attention-check questions. Group DASH-LSV rated debriefers lower than group DASH-SV across a multitude of DASH behaviors. Group DASH-LSV answered the attention check question correctly at a higher rate (91%) compared to group DASH-SV (82%) (p = 0.005). Our localized DASH-SV resulted in lower rates of score inflation compared to the original for select debriefing behaviors. Students who used the localized DASH-SV exhibited greater attentiveness. The localized DASH-SV may be a more accurate tool for student assessment of debriefing quality and support meaningful faculty feedback to improve debriefing skill and education quality.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40670-026-02825-1.

articles.title: Virtual Operating Theatre Simulation: Development and Evaluation of a Web-Based Learning Tool for Medical Students.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Preparing medical students for the operating theatre (OT) is challenging due to limited access and patient safety considerations. Virtual learning tools offer a safe and scalable method to introduce perioperative concepts. This study describes the development and evaluation of a web-based virtual OT program for undergraduate medical students.
METHODS: A mixed-methods evaluation was conducted with Year 3 and Year 5 medical students. Knowledge acquisition was assessed using pre- and post-tests, while perceptions were evaluated using a structured questionnaire and open-ended feedback. Internal consistency was examined using Cronbach's alpha, and quantitative analyses included paired and independent t-tests. Qualitative comments were descriptively grouped into themes.
RESULTS: Both cohorts demonstrated significant knowledge improvement following the virtual OT program (p < .001). Semester 9 students achieved higher post-test scores, reflecting the influence of prior clinical exposure. Perception scores were positive, with strong internal consistency for usability (α = 0.90), audio-visual quality (α = 0.93), and usefulness (α = 0.82). Qualitative feedback highlighted clarity, flexibility, and preparatory value as key strengths, while identifying glitches, image resolution, and device compatibility as areas for refinement.
DISCUSSION: The virtual OT program enhanced knowledge and was positively received as a preparatory and reinforcement tool. It aligns with global patient safety priorities and shows potential for broader adoption, including in nursing and interprofessional education.

articles.title: Virtual Reality as a Preparatory Educational Tool in Non-VR Trauma Simulation for Medical Students: A Qualitative Content Analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Simulation-based medical education (SMBE) is a well-established and effective method for clinical training, yet its implementation is often resource-intensive and logistically demanding. Virtual reality (VR) has emerged as a promising educational tool, offering immersive, multisensory simulations that may support both procedural and cognitive skill development. In educational context where students must prepare for complex scenarios, VR may serve as a preparatory educational tool. Thus, exploring such simulation formats is well justified to enhance training outcomes.
AIM: To explore medical students' experiences of using VR as preparation for a subsequent non-VR trauma simulation.
METHODS: Thirty-two medical students in their seventh semester who were assigned to use a VR application prior to a scheduled non-VR trauma simulation, participated in this study. Eight focus-group interviews were conducted immediately after the trauma simulation. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis.
RESULTS: The findings were categorised into four categories: Perceived educational effect, Practical user experience, Comparison of VR and other educational forms, and Areas for improvement in the VR application. The students described the VR application as an engaging and motivating learning method that supported autonomous preparation. However, the VR application was not perceived as sufficient to replace traditional educational formats. Key limitations included low interactivity, limited realism, and lack of cognitive flexibility. The participants proposed improvements, such as dynamic patient responses, expanded roles, and increased complexity in order to better reflect clinical practice.
CONCLUSIONS: The VR application shows potential as a flexible and accessible preparatory complement to SMBE. However, in its current form, it was not perceived as a suitable standalone learning method. The identified limitations relate to the design and scope of the specific VR application studied rather than to inherent limitations of VR technology. Student perspectives offer important insights into how preparatory VR may support motivation, early cognitive rehearsal and familiarization with simulation workflows, and should be actively considered in the development of VR-based educational tools.

articles.title: Beyond the Checklist: Developing Effective Communication in a South African Multilingual Clinical Training Programme.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Effective communication is a core graduate attribute (GA) in health professions education, yet its development is fragmented and under-theorised in under-resourced and multilingual contexts, which are typical of the Global South, where postcolonial histories and structural inequities continue to shape educational practice.
METHOD: We investigated how effective communication is understood, experienced and developed in a South African Clinical Technology programme, using a qualitative design underpinned by Engeström's Activity Theory as an interpretive lens. Interviews and focus groups were conducted with final-year students (n = 10), recent graduates (n = 5), academic educators (n = 4), and clinical educators (n = 6), and thematic analysis was applied.
RESULTS: Four themes emerged: (1) effective communication as a situated, adaptive practice; (2) Barriers to effective communication (linguistic, cultural, structural); (3) Role modelling and relational dynamics; and (4) Adaptability and resilience in workplace communication. Effective communication development was largely relational and experiential rather than shaped by formal curriculum, with students learning communication through immersion and mentorship amid systemic challenges. Structural misalignments between formal curricular goals and clinical realities constrained students' communication practice and confidence.
CONCLUSION: For educators, the findings suggest practical steps: 1) reconceptualise effective communication as a situated, socially mediated practice; (2) embed multilingual and multimodal communication opportunities into routine clinical teaching and assessment; (3) strengthen alignment and dialogue between universities and clinical training sites; and (4) prioritise faculty development to support inclusive role modelling and psychologically safe learning environments. Re-conceptualising effective communication as a situated, socially mediated practice (instead of a generic skill), enables intentional curriculum design and assessment that better prepare graduates for the complex socio-cultural clinical environments of the Global South.

articles.title: Gen Z Medical and Physician Assistant Student Recommendations for Medical School Wellness Programming.
articles.abstract: Despite medical school efforts to promote student wellness, more work is needed to better meet the needs of Generation Z medical learners, particularly in the post-COVID era. This study reports qualitative analysis of an open-ended question included in a larger anonymous online survey, exploring student perspectives regarding medical school-based wellness initiatives. A total of 1,423 students from 9 universities across the state of Florida [8 allopathic and 2 osteopathic medicine programs, and 4 physician assistant (PA) programs] completed the survey. Among respondents, 505 medical and 60 PA students offered comments specifically related to wellness programming/resources. Using thematic analysis, five major themes emerged: 1) enhance wellness activities, 2) revamp wellness education, 3) expand financial assistance, 4) enhance campus spaces and social interaction, and 5) expand access to mental healthcare. Students recommended schools: promote engaging structured activities supporting mental, emotional, and/or physical wellness; modify wellness education to enhance relevance, effectiveness, and engagement; reduce financial strain by offering targeted support for food, educational costs, and living expenses; create a supportive campus environment by improving physical spaces and fostering social connection; and provide better access to mental health counseling to help manage stress and other challenges. Student recommendations to support wellness varied in feasibility given resource constraints (i.e., limited time, lack of funding), highlighting the challenges faced by medical schools in supporting their learners. As medical schools consider implementing new programs or resources based on these recommendations, it will be important to evaluate and communicate the expected cost-benefit and applicable constraints.

articles.title: Shaping the future doctor: evaluating clinical competence, professionalism, and social accountability among the inaugural medical graduates of the university of global health equity, Rwanda.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Globally, medical education is shifting toward competency-based and socially accountable models that emphasize not only clinical proficiency but also ethical behavior and responsiveness to community needs. This shift must also address systemic challenges such as uneven supervision and limited clinical exposure. This study examined self-reported procedural confidence, stakeholder perceptions of clinical competence, professionalism, communication, and social accountability among the University of Global Health (UGHE) first cohort (2025) of medical graduates, who were trained under a competency-based, socially accountable curriculum.
METHODS: A mixed-methods cross-sectional study was conducted among interns, supervisors, nurses, and hospital directors at five hospitals representing both urban and rural contexts. A structured survey captured interns' self-reported procedural confidence across 48 core procedures, while 16 focus group discussions (≈22 h) explored stakeholder perceptions of interns' clinical performance, professionalism, teamwork, communication, and social accountability. Quantitative and qualitative data were analyzed through descriptive statistics and thematic analysis, respectively, and integrated through triangulation.
RESULTS: Interns reported moderate to high self-reported confidence in common routine and emergency procedures, including intravenous line insertion, wound care, infection prevention, oxygen administration, and patient stabilization. Lower confidence was reported for more complex or less frequently performed procedures, including lumbar puncture, pleural tap, fracture reduction, and vacuum-assisted delivery. Qualitative analysis generated four key themes: supervised clinical exposure as the foundation for procedural confidence; professionalism, humility, and respectful teamwork as markers of workplace readiness; socially accountable care through patient advocacy and adaptation to resource constraints; and interns' contribution to service delivery through improved communication, workflow, and team coordination. Across sites, supervisors and nursing leaders described interns as respectful, reliable, collaborative, ethical, and willing to seek guidance when faced with uncertainty. Limited exposure to advanced procedures and variability in supervision remained important challenges.
CONCLUSIONS: The study suggests that competency-based, socially accountable medical education can produce graduates who are perceived by colleagues and supervisors as clinically capable, ethically grounded, and able to contribute meaningfully to patient care and health-system functioning in resource-constrained settings. However, strengthening procedural confidence requires increased clinical exposure, structured supervision, timely feedback, and supportive workplace-based learning environments.

articles.title: How digitalisation and emerging artificial intelligence shape cultural adaptability and lifelong learning among postpartum caregivers: a qualitative study in southern China.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To explore how digitalisation and emerging artificial intelligence (AI) shape cultural adaptability and lifelong learning among professional postpartum caregivers (yuesao) in China.
DESIGN: A descriptive thematic qualitative study using semi-structured interviews, analysed through Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis and informed by cultural-historical activity theory.
SETTING: A vocational school specialising in postpartum healthcare in a coastal city of Guangdong Province, southern China.
PARTICIPANTS: We invited 16 practising yuesao (0.5–5 years of experience) and 5 trainers (3–10 years of experience). Participants were purposively sampled for diversity in age, educational level and years of experience. All had used Panda Cloud Classroom as part of their training.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
RESULTS: Three core themes emerged: (1) cultural adaptability as negotiated cultural capital in performing zuo yuezi, involving balancing tradition and modernity, regional knowledge and emotional labour; (2) hybrid digital—in-person training constrained by a persistent digital divide related to literacy and infrastructure and (3) informal and formal pathways for lifelong learning, including peer communities and certification programmes. Digital platforms improved access and flexibility, yet human instructors remained essential for resolving tradition-modernity tensions and managing emotional labour with families. Participants reported only minimal exposure to basic AI features such as content recommendations; their views on advanced applications (eg, regionally tailored adaptive systems) were therefore speculative and aspirational, not evidence of demonstrated benefit.
CONCLUSIONS: Digital tools enhance flexibility in yuesao training but cannot fully replace human instructors in culturally sensitive caregiving. Unresolved contradictions between national digitalisation policies and unequal infrastructure limit expansive learning. Findings support tiered digital literacy programmes and formalised mentorship rather than premature reliance on AI. Because this is a single-site qualitative study, the findings are transferable to similar contexts rather than generalisable. Future research should include employing families and cross-regional comparisons.

articles.title: Perceived Impact of Early On-Call Exposure on General Medical Council Outcomes Among Graduates: A Project in an English Foundation School.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Transitioning from medical school to Foundation training is widely recognised as a challenging stage, with new doctors often reporting underpreparedness for clinical responsibilities. Early exposure to on-call shifts during undergraduate training may help address this gap.
AIM: This study evaluated Foundation doctors' perceptions of how early on-call experience during United Kingdom medical school related to their preparedness and to their development of professional knowledge, skills, and values and behaviours, as defined in the General Medical Council Outcomes for Graduates.
METHODS: A convergent parallel mixed-methods design was used. A survey of 71 Foundation Year 1 doctors in an English Foundation School achieved 19 responses (26.7%). Quantitative data were collected using Likert-scale questions and analysed descriptively and with exploratory one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank tests against a neutral response, while qualitative data from open-ended questions underwent thematic analysis.
RESULTS: Of the 19 participants, 18 (94.7%) had undertaken on-call placements, predominantly in years 4 and 5. Perceptions were generally positive, with the highest mean Likert scores for knowledge (3.56) and skills (3.44), and lower scores for preparedness (3.22) and professional values (3.22); however, none of the four statements differed significantly from neutral (p = 0.057-0.235). Thematic analysis highlighted perceived benefits, including exposure to acute cases, improved confidence, and enhanced decision-making. Challenges included variability in supervision, limited teaching during night shifts, and difficulty adapting to out-of-hours schedules.
CONCLUSION: Respondents generally perceived undergraduate on-call exposure positively, particularly for knowledge and skills, although these findings were not statistically significant and views on professional values and behaviours were less consistent. Perceived educational value varied according to supervision and context. Larger comparative studies are needed to determine whether structured on-call placements improve preparedness.

articles.title: Pilot Mixed-Methods Evaluation of Simulation-Based Focused Cardiac Ultrasound Teaching for Final-Year Medical Students.
articles.abstract: Background Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is increasingly used within emergency and acute care, yet undergraduate exposure to focused bedside echocardiography remains variable. Simulation may provide an opportunity for students to develop practical ultrasound skills while integrating findings into clinical assessment and decision-making. This study evaluated the feasibility and acceptability of a simulation-based bedside echocardiography teaching programme for final-year medical students and explored differences in confidence and knowledge between pre- and post-session respondents. Methodology A mixed-methods educational evaluation was undertaken with final-year medical students during their Preparation for Practice placement at a UK teaching hospital. The two-hour programme combined teaching on ultrasound principles and standard echocardiographic views with supervised image acquisition and simulation-based peri-arrest scenarios involving cardiac arrest, massive pulmonary embolism and pericardial tamponade. Thirty students were invited and 10 attended. Anonymous questionnaires assessed self-reported confidence and knowledge immediately before and after the session, and a five-question multiple-choice quiz objectively assessed knowledge. We also collected qualitative free-text feedback post-session. Confidence reflected participants' own perceived confidence across three domains of bedside echocardiography and was not assessed externally or used as a measure of objective competence. As questionnaires were anonymous, pre- and post-session responses were unpaired. Self-reported confidence scores were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test. Results Nine students completed the pre-session questionnaire, and seven completed the post-session questionnaire. Mean confidence scores were higher among post-session respondents (9.86/15; median, 10) than among pre-session respondents (3.67/15; median, 4), with a statistically significant difference between groups (U = 0.0, P < 0.001). Mean knowledge scores were also higher among post-session respondents (4.71/5 vs. 4.22/5), although baseline scores were already high. Qualitative feedback was positive, with students particularly valuing the clinical relevance of the teaching and the integration of echocardiography into realistic emergency scenarios. Participants identified additional supervised scanning opportunities as an area for future development. Conclusions This preliminary evaluation suggests that a short, simulation-based bedside echocardiography teaching programme is feasible to deliver within an undergraduate prep-for-practice placement and acceptable to participating final-year medical students. Higher confidence and knowledge scores were observed among post-session respondents; however, the small sample size and unpaired questionnaire design prevent conclusions regarding individual learner improvement or intervention efficacy. Larger studies incorporating paired responses, objective assessment of ultrasound competence and longitudinal follow-up are required to evaluate the effectiveness and retention of this educational approach.

articles.title: Medical Students' Perceptions of Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Large Language Models: Dyadic Interview and Exploratory Survey Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: There is evidence of rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) in undergraduate medical education, with medical students using them to support their learning. This raises concerns about the accuracy of LLM-generated information that students are learning from. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which grounds an LLM in curated materials, may be a strategy to improve the accuracy of this information.
OBJECTIVE: This study explored medical students' perceptions after using an online tool, NotebookLM, that uses RAG.
METHODS: A cohort of 284 second-year medical students at Bristol Medical School were encouraged to use NotebookLM over a period of 4 months (March 2025 to June 2025) to help them learn course content. Following this, volunteers were recruited to share their perspectives through interviews and a survey that was open for 4 months (June 2025 to September 2025). A total of 9 individuals participated: 2 through interviews and 7 through the survey. Qualitative data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and supplemented by Likert scale data.
RESULTS: NotebookLM was perceived as more reliable than standard LLM responses by interview participants, mainly due to the transparency of and control over information sources. Reliability ratings from survey participants were more mixed, but none rated unreliable. Students described it as an accessible, on-demand learning resource, which they perceived as improving efficiency and supporting self-directed study. They reported continued use of strategies to cross-check generated information. Participants demonstrated some awareness of ethical concerns, but it was unclear whether this altered their practice.
CONCLUSIONS: In this small, exploratory study, students described NotebookLM as improving trust in LLM outputs while maintaining their flexibility. The findings suggest that RAG may be a strategy to support students who use LLMs. However, further research is needed to formally evaluate RAG vs standard LLMs, including the impact of RAG on accuracy, curricular alignment, and the ability of students to meet learning outcomes.
