articles.title: When Words Shape Care: Educating First-Year Medical Students on Identifying and Replacing Bias in Electronic Health Documentation.
articles.journal: MedEdPORTAL : the journal of teaching and learning resources
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Although medical education increasingly addresses bias in patient care, less attention has been paid to biased language in clinical documentation within the Electronic Health Record (EHR), a critical concern as patients have increasing access to their records. Because biased language can influence clinicians' perceptions and negatively affect patient relationships, focused medical student training is needed to promote equitable, patient-centered care.
METHODS: We implemented a one-hour workshop on biased language in medical records using case-based discussions. First-year students (MS1s) completed pre- and postsurveys assessing their ability to identify biased language. Results were analyzed using paired t-tests, descriptive statistics, and thematic analysis.
RESULTS: Sixty-nine MS1s attended the workshop; 68 completed the presurvey (98.5%), and 63 the postsurvey (91.3%). Students demonstrated significant improvement in their ability to identify biased language in patient cases (P < .001) and survey scores (P < .001). Significant improvements were also observed in students' ability to identify the word "claims" as biased language (P < .001), identify language that defined patients by their illness (P < .001), and recognize negative patient descriptions (P < .001). Students valued the workshop's use of examples of biased language and neutral language alternatives, and many recommended incorporating this training into the medical school curriculum.
DISCUSSION: The workshop improved MS1s' recognition of biased language in EHR documentation. Incorporating documentation bias training early in medical school may strengthen students' awareness of biased language and support more patient-centered documentation.

articles.title: Psychiatric education in medical training: a scoping review of curricular innovations, teaching strategies, and assessment methods.
articles.journal: International journal of mental health systems
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Mental disorders contribute substantially to global disease burden, yet persistent deficiencies remain in medical trainees' readiness to identify, diagnose, and treat patients with mental health conditions. Main barriers include stigma, outdated curricula, insufficient clinical practice, and regional differences in mental health services.
OBJECTIVES: This scoping review systematically mapped existing research on educational innovations, learning approaches, and evaluation instruments in psychiatric education for medical learners (2015-2026), with formal quality appraisal using a JBI-adapted tool.
METHODS: Following JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a systematic search was conducted across MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and Scopus. The PCC model guided eligibility. Two reviewers independently selected articles and extracted data. A ten-item JBI-adapted quality appraisal checklist was applied to all included studies. The evidence base comprised 34 primary empirical studies (77.3%) and 10 secondary or contextual sources (22.7%).
RESULTS: Of 3,682 articles identified, 44 met inclusion criteria 34 primary empirical studies (77.3%) and 10 secondary sources (22.7%). Most originated from the United States (54.5%), focusing on undergraduate learners (88.6%). Quality appraisal revealed only 34.1% used validated measures, 20.5% included follow-up, and 18.2% fully met control group criteria. Thematic analysis identified five themes: curricular innovations, educational approaches, assessment methods, Kirkpatrick-classified outcomes, and implementation barriers/facilitators. While all 44 reported Level 1 and Level 2 outcomes, measured in primary studies and discussed in secondary sources, no studies measured Level 3 behavioral change or Level 4 patient outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: The absence of Level 3 and Level 4 evidence represents a major limitation and priority for future research; it does not imply health systems cannot invest in psychiatric education, but that the evidence base has not yet demonstrated translation to improved clinical behaviors or patient outcomes. Future research should prioritize longitudinal and system-level evaluation with validated behavioral and patient-level outcome measures.

articles.title: Fostering empathy and narrative competence through oral history videos in community-based medical education: a mixed-methods study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Empathy and narrative competence are essential components of patient-centered care and professional identity formation in medical education. However, empathy often declines during medical training, and conventional communication programs may foster performed rather than authentic empathy. Narrative medicine offers a promising framework for cultivating humanistic understanding in medical education. Central to this approach is narrative competence, defined as the ability to recognize, absorb, interpret, and act upon the stories of others. This study explored how viewing and discussing oral history videos of local older adults could foster empathy and narrative competence among medical students in a community-based educational context.
METHODS: A convergent mixed-methods design with qualitative priority was employed. Twenty-seven fifth- and sixth-year medical students at Tottori University participated in a 60-minute session during their one-week community-based clinical placement. Participants viewed a 20-minute oral history video from a regional series featuring older residents' life stories, followed by a reflective group discussion. Empathy was assessed using the Japanese version of the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI) before and after the session. Written reflections were thematically analyzed to explore experiential learning.
RESULTS: The total IRI score showed a small, non-significant increase (91.25 to 92.69; t = 0.82, p = 0.42, Cohen's d = 0.15). Thematic analysis identified nine categories, including recognizing the significance of listening to narratives, respecting individuality, recognizing patients' social and historical contexts, and reconsidering assumptions about older adults and patient care. Students described emotional resonance, reflective insight, and renewed awareness of patients' values and life histories.
CONCLUSIONS: Although quantitative measures revealed minimal change, qualitative findings suggested short-term reflective engagement with patients' life histories, values, and social contexts. Oral history-based narrative education may enrich community-based medical training by linking empathy, reflection, and narrative listening, and may offer a concise approach for supporting context-sensitive, patient-centered care.

articles.title: MassCas tabletop game as a training tool in mass casualty incidents for undergraduate medical students: a quasi-experimental study with knowledge assessment at 6-month follow-up.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Mass casualty incidents (MCI) require a coordinated prehospital response from multiple healthcare teams. Undergraduate medical students rarely receive systematic MCI training, and some of the methods that have shown good results so far, full-scale simulations and extended reality (XR), tend to be expensive, logistically demanding, and not always reproducible across centres. The aim is to measure the change in knowledge scores from baseline to 6-month follow-up after a brief, low-cost gamified tabletop session, including the differential effect of sex and active role assignment, and to measure student experience with the game.
METHODS: Quasi-experimental, single-group pretest/follow-up study with a knowledge assessment six months after the intervention; no immediate post-intervention knowledge test was administered. A total of 119 medical students from the Universidad de Oviedo took part in a 2-hour session using the MassCas tabletop game. Self-perception was measured with a 27-item self-efficacy questionnaire (Cronbach α = 0.926), covering methodology, knowledge acquisition, and skills acquisition (Likert 1-10). A 10-item knowledge test was administered before (n = 119) and six months after the session (n = 95), without any study material in between. Attrition was assessed by comparing measured baseline characteristics between respondents and non-respondents to the 6-month assessment. Effect sizes were calculated as r (Wilcoxon) and Cohen's d. Sex and role assignment (active vs. passive) were explored as subgroup factors.
RESULTS: Self-efficacy scores were high in all three dimensions: methodology (Median = 10; IQR = 2), knowledge acquisition (Median = 10; IQR = 1), and skills acquisition (Median = 9; IQR = 2). Knowledge scores were markedly higher at 6-month follow-up than at baseline: median pre-test 4 (IQR = 2) versus post-test 7 (IQR = 2); Wilcoxon p < 0.001, r = 0.76, d = 1.19 (95% CI: 0.86-1.54). Among 63 email-matched pairs, 88.9% improved (r = 0.81, d = 1.44). Respondents and non-respondents to the post-test did not differ in pre-test score, sex, age, or role assignment (all p > 0.10), with respect to these measured characteristics; differences in unmeasured characteristics cannot be excluded. Students with an active role rated methodology and skills dimensions somewhat higher; the largest difference was found for leadership (p = 0.007). Female students rated methodology slightly higher than males (p = 0.006). No statistically significant differences in 6-month knowledge scores were detected by role or sex. Prior MCI training hours were not related to self-efficacy scores. Qualitative analysis pointed to interactivity, visual format, and practical applicability as the main strengths, while excessive group size was the most frequently mentioned weakness.
CONCLUSIONS: After a single 2-hour session with the MassCas tabletop game, knowledge scores in undergraduate medical students were substantially higher at 6-month follow-up than at baseline, without any study material provided in between (d = 1.19), together with highly favorable self-reported perceptions of the methodology and of knowledge and skills acquisition. A low-cost, logistically simple methodology that does not require specialized equipment may be a feasible option where resources are limited. Active role assignment was associated with slightly higher skills perception, while no statistically significant difference in 6-month knowledge scores was detected between active and passive participants. These findings support further evaluation and implementation of gamified tabletop exercises in undergraduate medical curricula as an accessible and potentially scalable strategy for MCI preparedness.

articles.title: Negotiating obligation and aspiration over time: A longitudinal qualitative study of regional quota medical students' reflective accounts.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Regional quota programmes recruit medical students to address geographic physician maldistribution, but attached service obligations can complicate career and professional identity development. Little is known about how students negotiate a professional future that is partly structured in advance. Understanding this process may help educators support career development without equating commitment with compliance. We examined how regional quota medical students represent and renegotiate service obligations, professional aspirations, and possible professional selves over time.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective longitudinal qualitative study of 560 required reflective reports from 239 students at Tottori University, Japan, collected from 2022 to 2025. Using the Framework Method, we combined inductive thematic analysis with case-by-time matrices and in-depth longitudinal analysis of 25 students who submitted reports in each of the four years. Professional identity formation and self-determination theory informed interpretation after theme development.
RESULTS: Three interrelated themes were identified: broadening community medicine beyond disease and location to persons, lives, communities, and systems; encounters making future professional selves imaginable; and conditional ownership, in which students reclaimed agency within service constraints without necessarily resolving ambivalence. Longitudinal cases showed deepening of existing commitments, reframing after encounters with credible role models, and persistent negotiation rather than a single developmental sequence.
DISCUSSION: Educational programmes linked to service obligations may be most constructive when they make career options visible, provide credible role models, and allow students to question constraints while developing personally meaningful professional plans.

articles.title: Gamified Formative Assessment in a First-Year Medical Morphology Course: Qualitative Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Formative assessment plays a central role in medical education by offering low-risk practice and timely feedback, particularly in visually and practically demanding courses, such as morphology. Gamified digital tools can foster active learning; however, their educational value relies on pedagogical integration rather than technology alone. The Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) model provides a framework for understanding this relationship.
OBJECTIVE: This study explored students' and a teacher's perceptions of Kahoot! as a gamified formative assessment tool in a first-year medical morphology course, identifying facilitators, tensions, and perceived educational value through the TPACK framework.
METHODS: This qualitative, exploratory study adopted an interpretive phenomenological orientation. It was conducted within the framework of the RAÍCES 2 (Red de ayudantes de investigación comprometidos con la educación en salud; Network of Student Researchers Committed to Health Professions Education) educational research project at Universidad San Sebastián (Valdivia, Chile). Kahoot! was implemented at the end of class sessions to simulate the visual and time demands of authentic practical examinations. Data collection included 2 online focus groups with first-year medical students (n=14) and 1 semistructured interview with the course teacher (n=1). Transcripts were analyzed using deductive coding informed by the TPACK framework and the project's analytical axes, combined with reflexive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke. ATLAS.ti was used to support the analysis.
RESULTS: Six interrelated themes emerged: (1) techno-disciplinary alignment, reflecting the value of authentic, high-resolution anatomical images and time constraints mirroring practical examinations; (2) Kahoot! as a formative closure, serving as an exit check that guided self-assessment and the identification of learning gaps; (3) from score to learning, highlighting the importance of immediate postquestion instructor feedback explaining both correct and incorrect answers; (4) motivation and socioemotional climate, whereby gamification enhanced engagement but triggered evaluative anxiety and leaderboard frustration, which were buffered by participant anonymity; (5) implementation conditions, mediated by connectivity, device availability, and time allocation; and (6) projection and improvement, highlighting the need for institutional question repositories and systematic curriculum integration.
CONCLUSIONS: Kahoot! effectively functions as a formative assessment strategy when intentionally aligned with disciplinary and practical evaluative demands. Its educational value is not inherent to the software but is determined by explicit pedagogical mediation and careful attention to students' socioemotional dynamics.

articles.title: Developing a Conceptual Academic Governance Framework for Faculty Evaluation in Medical Universities Based on a Critical Review.
articles.journal: Medical journal of the Islamic Republic of Iran
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Effective faculty evaluation is critical for quality assurance and professional development in medical universities; however, prevalent systems often lack integration, transparency, and contextual sensitivity-particularly in settings such as Iran. This study addresses this research gap by proposing a comprehensive, locally adapted framework aimed at enhancing evaluation practices and strengthening the connections between assessment, academic governance, and faculty growth.
METHODS: A critical review methodology was employed, following the four-stage framework established by Carnwell and Daly (2001). A systematic literature search was conducted across international databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, Google Scholar) and national databases (SID, Magiran, IranMedex) for studies published between 2000 and 2025. Search terms covered faculty evaluation, performance, appraisal, assessment, and teaching effectiveness, combined with terms related to medical education, medical schools, academic medicine, and health professions education. Thematic analysis was used forthe conceptual synthesis of existing faculty evaluation systems to develop an evidence-based model.
RESULTS: Analysis of eight international and national frameworks-including the AAMC Mission-Based management (MBM) model, Merit Review system, University of Minnesota multi-track system, MCDA, BSC-AHP-TOPSIS hybrid model, Textual Feedback Analysis Model, S-UDLCD data-driven model, and Iran's SHOA system-revealed that no single model was sufficient. Mission-based, merit-oriented, and data-driven systems each offered only partial strengths, with notable limitations in addressing the multidimensional nature of faculty roles, ensuring organizational justice, and linking evaluation to professional development and governance. Findings underscore the necessity for a hybrid, context-specific system that integrates quantitative, qualitative, and multi-source evidence.
CONCLUSION: A localized, mission-aligned, multi-criteria, and feedback-driven academic governance framework is proposed. This integrated model is organized around four key features: (1) explicit alignment of academic pathways with institutional missions, (2) integration of both quantitative and qualitative performance indicators, (3) multi-source assessment mechanisms that combine electronic data, structured weighting, and textual feedback analysis, and (4) a continuous feedback and development cycle that links evaluation outcomes to annual academic contracts, resource allocation, and promotion decisions. This model provides a foundation for educational policymakers and university administrators to design fair, transparent, and development-oriented evaluation systems. Future studies should focus on pilot implementation, empirical validation of the model in Iranian medical universities, and longitudinal assessment of its impact on faculty performance, satisfaction, and institutional outcomes.

articles.title: From observation to participation: a needs assessment of clinical clerkship in Korean medicine toward competency-based education.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Health professions education is shifting from simple observation to competency-based education, and Korean Medicine is no exception. Clerkship is increasingly regarded as the stage at which students acquire the competencies needed to deliver primary care independently. However, what learners experience and require in clerkship remains largely unexamined in traditional medicine. This study identified the current state of clerkship education and learner needs at a college of Korean Medicine and explored the causes and solutions to the problems it uncovered.
METHODS: We used an explanatory mixed-methods design with partially overlapping data collection, grounded in pragmatism. Forty-two fourth-year students who had completed a clerkship at the College of Korean Medicine, Wonkwang University, completed a survey in 2025; seven survey respondents also participated in in-depth interviews. Preliminary survey responses informed the interview guide, and the qualitative findings were used to explain and contextualize the quantitative results. Paired t-tests were used to examine importance-performance gaps across five competency domains (history taking, physical examination and diagnostic testing, communication skills, clinical reasoning and treatment planning, and clinical skills). Priorities were derived using the Borich needs assessment and the Locus for Focus model. Interview data underwent thematic analysis structured according to educational content, methods, and environment.
RESULTS: Most respondents (83.3%) were satisfied with clerkship education, yet 42.9% considered change necessary, most often citing "variation in clerkship across departments." Performance fell below the importance level in all five domains. Borich priorities ranked communication skills the first, followed by clinical skills. The Locus for Focus model placed physical examination and diagnostic testing in the highest-priority quadrant. The interviews identified four issues: limited participation in patient care, the absence of a systematic communication curriculum, too few opportunities for repeated skills practice, and variations in clerkship delivery across hospitals and departments.
CONCLUSIONS: Clerkship education in colleges of Korean Medicine may benefit from moving beyond passive observation toward structured participation and competency-focused training centered on communication and clinical skills. These findings offer an empirical basis for identifying priority areas in clerkship redesign and serve as foundational evidence for informing future competency-based clerkship development in traditional medicine.

articles.title: Stakeholder perspectives on the Emirati board comprehensive clinical examination: a mixed-methods multi-stakeholder evaluation.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: High-stakes clinical examinations play a critical role in postgraduate medical training by assessing readiness for independent specialist practice. While hybrid Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE)-style assessments are increasingly used to evaluate integrated clinical competence, evidence incorporating the perspectives of multiple stakeholders remains limited, particularly in large-scale specialist certification examinations. Multi-stakeholder evaluations may provide valuable insights into examination quality, implementation, and stakeholder experience.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate stakeholder perceptions of the Emirati Board Comprehensive Clinical Examination (CCE) across key domains, including orientation, logistics, educational value, task clarity, examiner behaviour, and overall examination experience, and to identify implementation factors that may influence perceived examination quality.
METHODS: A convergent mixed-methods study was conducted using repeated cross-sectional stakeholder feedback collected across multiple CCE examination sittings between November 2024 and January 2026. Quantitative data were obtained from post-examination surveys completed by examinees (n = 368), examiners (n = 390), and quality assessors (QA; n = 88), supplemented by post-examination debriefing notes from all stakeholders. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics and group comparisons, while qualitative data underwent thematic analysis. Findings from both data strands were integrated during interpretation.
RESULTS: Examiners and quality assessors reported consistently positive perceptions of the examination (mean scores 4.4-4.8 out of 5), whereas examinees reported more moderate ratings (overall mean 3.88 out of 5), particularly regarding orientation, logistics, and task clarity. Qualitative findings complemented these results by identifying perceived variability in task instructions, time allocation, examiner interactions, and simulated patient performance. Integration of quantitative and qualitative findings indicated broad agreement regarding the educational value and overall organization of the examination, while also highlighting differences between system-level evaluations and examinees' lived experiences.
CONCLUSION: The Emirati Board CCE was generally perceived as a well-organized and educationally valuable assessment by all stakeholder groups. However, examinees reported greater variability in their examination experience than examiners and quality assessors, particularly in domains related to orientation, logistics, and task clarity. These findings suggest that enhancing consistency in examination implementation may improve stakeholder experience, perceived fairness, and future quality improvement initiatives in high-stakes clinical assessment.

articles.title: Mixed-reality-assisted training for vascular anastomosis: An exploratory pilot study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This exploratory pilot study aimed to explore the feasibility of mixed reality (MR)-assisted vascular anastomosis training for clinical clerks and to obtain preliminary data on technical performance and learner experience compared with conventional instruction using illustrated handouts.
METHODS: Twelve fifth-year medical students were assigned to either the MR group (n = 6), which used a head-mounted display, or the control group (n = 6), which used printed handouts. After a standardized lecture, participants performed end-to-side vascular anastomosis twice using latex grafts. Technical performance was assessed using a 10-item original scale informed by the Objective Structured Assessment of Technical Skills and the End-Product Rating Score. Subjective feedback was collected after each session using a paper-based, author-developed questionnaire.
RESULTS: Total scores did not differ significantly between the two groups in either the first session (28.3 ± 3.1 vs 32.0 ± 2.5, p = 0.106) or the second session (31.8 ± 2.8 vs 30.7 ± 1.7, p = 0.467). The total score increased within the MR group (p = 0.034), although the between-group difference in score change was not statistically significant (p = 0.263). Questionnaire responses indicated greater initial mental fatigue in the MR group, which decreased with repeated use.
CONCLUSIONS: This exploratory pilot study provides preliminary support for the practical feasibility of incorporating MR-assisted guidance into vascular anastomosis training. Initial mental fatigue and possible device-familiarization effects are practical considerations. Larger, adequately powered studies are needed to determine the comparative educational efficacy of MR.

articles.title: Bridging Simulation and Practice: Designing, Implementing, and Evaluating a Curriculum for Educating Medical Students as Robotic Surgery Bedside Assistants.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medical students often face limited involvement in robotic surgery, leading to unfulfilling learning experiences. Establishing a defined role for students in the operating room (OR) can enhance their engagement and deepen their understanding of robotic surgery. We describe the design and implementation of a curriculum designed to train medical students as robotic surgery bedside assistants and explore the perspectives of key stakeholders involved in the program.
METHODS: We designed a curriculum based on Kern's 6-step approach for curricular development. It included a series of online modules and a simulated hands-on session, followed by case assignments over their 4-week rotation. The curriculum centered on training students in an asset of core bedside skills that had been identified in a previous study. Students initially received supervision in the OR and progressed toward increasing autonomy. Fourth-year medical students could participate during their surgical subinternships. Major stakeholders, including students, residents, faculty, and OR staff participated in semistructured interviews to share their experiences; transcripts were subsequently analyzed using qualitative methods.
RESULTS: Fourteen students participated and were interviewed. Students valued their defined roles, experiential learning, and interprofessional collaboration, noting increased engagement and confidence. Stakeholders (n = 13) reported that the curriculum enhanced medical student readiness for surgical training by fostering technical skill development, professional integration, and increased autonomy. Residents and faculty observed that students functioned at or near intern level by the end of the rotation and appreciated how student involvement at the bedside supported resident console time. OR staff and faculty acknowledged early implementation challenges, including staff unfamiliarity, but noted that improved communication and onboarding processes helped address these barriers.
CONCLUSIONS: The robotic bedside assist curriculum was perceived to support safe, structured, and inclusive learning while promoting student development within the surgical team, giving students a legitimate role in robotic surgery.

articles.title: Perceived barriers and facilitators to medical students participating in volunteer services for older adults with disabilities: a qualitative descriptive study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: With global aging accelerating, volunteer services have become a cornerstone for sustaining care for older adults with disabilities (older adults aged 60 and above with age-related functional limitations). Medical students play a unique role in this system due to their professional competencies. However, they encounter particular environmental and psychological pressures that impact their sustained engagement. Existing literature has mostly focused on general motivations, while the barriers and facilitators influencing sustained participation have not been sufficiently explored through the application of a theoretical framework. This study aims to explore the facilitators and barriers of medical students participating in volunteer services for older adults with disabilities.
METHODS: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted using purposive sampling from two medical schools in Southwest China. Sixteen semi-structured interviews were conducted between October 2025 and January 2026 based on the Capability, Opportunity, and Motivation-Behavior (COM-B) model. Data analysis utilized the framework approach, with the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) used to map behavioral factors.
RESULTS: Analysis revealed nine core themes regarding medical students' perceptions of the barriers and facilitators to volunteering with older adults with disabilities within the COM-B model and the TDF framework. Facilitators included strong professional identity and empathy, social influence and interpersonal support, and incentive structures with career ambitions. Barriers were identified as the gap between theoretical knowledge and practice, physical stamina, and emergency decision-making pressures, information accessibility issues, resource limitations, and emotional experiences, coupled with psychological obstacles. A dilemma of "high intention, low efficacy" was observed.
CONCLUSION: The present findings highlight the complex relationship between students' professional aspirations and practical constraints and could contribute to the development of more effective volunteer service models for older adults with disabilities. Medical educational institutions and community organizations should implement simulation-based training to bridge the theory-practice gap, establish psychological support systems to enhance resilience, and optimize resource allocation. These measures are necessary to transform medical students' motivation into sustainable practical capability.

articles.title: Designing transformative sustainability education: a mixed methods study exploring the values and perspectives of medical students.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Education for Sustainable Healthcare (ESH) is a novel area of medical education and high-quality evidence to guide effective learning approaches is yet to be established. This study investigates the design of ESH in undergraduate medicine through the lenses of transformative learning, environmental value position and student-centred design.
METHODS: A mixed methods approach was used. A questionnaire assessed the environmental value position and attitudes towards ESH of undergraduate medical students at the University of Dundee. Semi-structured interviews with a sub-group of these students further evaluated environmental perspectives and explored preferences for learning approaches for ESH.
RESULTS: The questionnaire data indicated that the students had high levels of environmental concern, arising from an ecocentric value position. Ecocentrism correlated with support for the integration of ESH and sustainability in medicine. The qualitative findings from 10 interviews confirmed high levels of environmental concern and support for ESH but suggested a more complex underlying value basis. There was a disconnection between students' environmental values and their engagement with sustainable medical practice, arising from conflict between their sense of medical professionalism and aspects of sustainable medical practice that were perceived to be at odds with providing optimal patient care. Regarding learning approaches, students highlighted the need to prioritise examined content, and reported a preference for small group, interactive learning, delivered by engaged tutors in an authentic and relevant way.
DISCUSSION: It is important that the integration of ESH involves summative assessment; without this, students are unlikely to engage with the topic. ESH learning approaches should be designed in accordance with student preferences if they are to maximise impact: interactive, student-centred, experiential learning approaches are preferred. ESH should bridge the gap between students' environmental attitudes and capacities for sustainable behaviour by empowering them to act sustainably through role modelling, skills acquisition, project work and critical reflection.

articles.title: Bridging theory and practice in medical education: evaluating a faculty development masterclass using a commitment-to-change framework in a resource-variable setting.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite advances in medical education, translating educational theory into routine teaching practice remains challenging. Faculty development programs often demonstrate high participant satisfaction but limited evidence of behavior change. The Commitment-to-Change (CtC) framework offers a method for evaluating whether educational interventions lead to practice modification. This study evaluated whether a theory-informed faculty development masterclass grounded in cognitive science and instructional design principles could promote early implementation of evidence-based teaching strategies among medical educators.
METHODS: We conducted a prospective, multi-stage evaluation of a two-session synchronous virtual faculty development masterclass delivered through the Society of Experimental and Clinical Anatomical Scientists of Nigeria (SECAN). Current and aspiring medical and allied health educators from multiple institutions were recruited through SECAN's professional networks using email and social media. Data were collected electronically using online surveys, including a pre-masterclass needs assessment, post-session knowledge and application readiness assessment with CtC elicitation, post-masterclass evaluation, and a four-week follow-up survey assessing implementation and sustainability intentions. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, and qualitative responses were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis.
RESULTS: Ninety-two participants completed the pre-masterclass survey, with 42 attending the sessions. Eighteen participants completed the knowledge and readiness assessment, achieving a mean score of 79.2%. All participants (100%) articulated at least one CtC statement. Fifteen participants completed the post-masterclass evaluation, with high overall ratings (mean 4.62/5) and a Net Promoter Score of + 93.3. At four weeks, 12 participants responded to follow-up; 75.0% reported attempting their committed teaching change, and 91.7% indicated plans to sustain or scale the change. Implementation was reported across large-group, small-group, laboratory, and online teaching settings, although contextual barriers including time constraints, limited resources, and institutional factors were commonly identified.
CONCLUSIONS: A brief, theory-informed faculty development masterclass incorporating structured application and CtC elicitation was associated with high levels of participant satisfaction, strong intention to change, and substantial early implementation of teaching strategies. These findings suggest that short-duration, theory-informed faculty development interventions incorporating structured application and CtC activities can facilitate the early translation of learning science principles into teaching practice, even in resource-variable settings. Future work should examine long-term sustainability and institutional factors influencing adoption.

articles.title: Generative AI Factors, Cognitive Engagement, and Patient Safety Learning in Medical Education: Mixed Methods Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used during medical training, including clerkships in which learning takes place alongside supervised patient care. Its educational value may depend on how students interpret, verify, and regulate AI-generated output.
OBJECTIVE: This study explored medical clerkship students' accounts of GenAI use and examined how GenAI-related factors were associated with self-reported ward-based infection-prevention practice through self-efficacy in AI-generated usage and perceived AI self-control balance.
METHODS: We used an exploratory sequential mixed methods design. Eight medical clerkship students with experience using GenAI participated in semistructured interviews analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The qualitative findings were considered alongside theory and prior evidence to specify a theory-based model. This model was subsequently examined through an online cross-sectional survey of 214 eligible students recruited from 5 private universities in the Jakarta Metropolitan Area, Indonesia. Quantitative associations were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling with bootstrapping.
RESULTS: The interviews yielded 16 themes concerning appraisal of AI-generated output, confidence in using GenAI, interaction control, patient-safety awareness, and infection-prevention learning. The structural paths were unchanged, although 3 low-loading measurement indicators were removed before hypothesis testing. Global model fit was limited (estimated-model standardized root mean square residual 0.089; normed fit index 0.691), and pairwise residual fit was not used as a retention criterion. Explainability quality exposure and perceived algorithmic fairness were positively associated with both self-efficacy and perceived AI self-control balance. Trust calibration literacy was associated with self-efficacy but not perceived AI self-control balance. Privacy concern was positively associated with self-efficacy (β=0.294, P<.001), contrary to the hypothesized direction, but not with perceived AI self-control balance. Self-efficacy (β=0.477, P<.001) and perceived AI self-control balance (β=0.407, P<.001) were positively associated with self-reported ward-based infection-prevention practice; the model explained 51.9% of its variance. Specific indirect effects through self-efficacy were observed for all 4 antecedents and through perceived AI self-control balance only for explainability and fairness. A small positive interaction was observed between promotion of patient safety and self-efficacy (β=0.122, P=.04); the corresponding interaction involving perceived AI self-control balance was not observed.
CONCLUSIONS: Self-efficacy was the more consistent pathway linking students' appraisals of GenAI with self-reported ward-based infection-prevention practice. By integrating students' accounts with quantitative testing of a theory-based model, this study extends research that has largely focused on GenAI acceptance and general educational use by examining a safety-oriented outcome within clinical training. The findings add evidence on the human factors through which GenAI use may relate to patient-safety learning, although the cross-sectional, self-reported data do not establish causal or clinical effects. Medical schools and teaching hospitals could use these findings to inform clerkship guidance on supervised verification of AI-generated output, patient-data protection, alignment with local protocols, and continued human responsibility for clinical decisions.

articles.title: Large Language Model-Powered 3D Avatars to Train Shared Decision-Making in Undergraduate Medical Students: Design and Mixed Methods Acceptance Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Shared decision-making (SDM) is a core competency in patient-centered care, yet it is challenging for physicians. Simulation-based education with standardized patients (SPs) offers valuable practice opportunities for undergraduate medical education (UME), but is limited by cost, scalability, and variable feedback quality. Advances in large language model (LLM) technology and virtual patient (VP) design present a promising pathway toward accessible, realistic, and high-quality SDM skill training.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to develop LLM-powered, real-time interactive 3D avatars for SDM training in UME and to evaluate their acceptance among undergraduate medical students.
METHODS: We conducted a descriptive, cross-sectional mixed methods study at KU Leuven, Belgium (November-December 2025). The avatar system was developed through an iterative, interdisciplinary collaboration between medical educators, SDM experts, software developers, user experience designers, and AI engineers, grounded in prior work on physicians' educational needs and SDM learning mechanisms. Development comprised prototype case authoring, usability testing with medical students, and iterative refinement. The final system is a web-based platform featuring real-time, LLM-powered spoken dialogue with diverse, photorealistic 3D patient avatars; layered prompts configuring avatar personality, clinical scenario, and difficulty; an educator panel for case authoring; and automated AI-generated formative feedback structured around 6 phases of SDM. After using the system for 1 month, a convenience sample of UME students completed a 9-item, 5-point Likert scale questionnaire grounded in the technology acceptance model (TAM), assessing perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and intention to use. Optional open-text responses were narratively analyzed to triangulate these findings.
RESULTS: Of 25 recruited participants, 24 were included in the analysis. Internal consistency was acceptable for perceived usefulness (α=0.76) and intention to use (α=0.78), but not for perceived ease of use (α=0.69). All construct means exceeded the scale midpoint of 3, suggesting high overall acceptance. Students rated perceived usefulness highest (mean 4.43, SD 0.50), followed by intention to use (mean 4.42, SD 0.59), and perceived ease of use was the lowest (mean 3.81, SD 0.68). Fourteen participants provided open-text responses. These highlighted the value of a safe, low-pressure environment for practicing communication without patients or peers present; reported mixed experiences with avatar realism, with reservations directed at behavioral rather than physical realism; and identified technical difficulties (microphone issues, freezing, and crashes) as the most frequent area for improvement.
CONCLUSIONS: LLM-powered, real-time interactive 3D avatars are feasible and well-accepted tools for SDM training in UME. Students found the system educationally valuable and intended to use it again. Technical reliability and behavioral realism should be prioritized in future development. The modular architecture and automated feedback pipeline support scalable deployment across disciplines, institutions, and languages. Larger, multi-institutional studies with objective learning outcome measures are needed to establish efficacy.

articles.title: Teaching medical care in mass casualty incidents through advanced clinical simulation.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The threat of intentional mass casualty incidents remains high, making healthcare response a priority. The Hartford Consensus and the THREAT protocol (Threat suppression, Hemorrhage control, Rapid Extrication to safety, Assessment by medical providers, Transport to definitive care) establish recommended actions. A key objective is training civilians as "immediate responders" for hemorrhage control. However, this emergency care training is often limited in medical schools. Francisco de Vitoria University incorporates clinical simulation, including emergency medicine content in the fifth year. This study aims to assess learning outcomes from an activity designed to familiarize students with the Hartford Consensus and THREAT protocol.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Simulation Activity Development: Students gathered in an enclosed area. Basic principles of action during a terrorist attack were explained. A simulated attack unfolded, requiring students to escape, hide, or fight, and assist victims according to protocol. Wounded individuals were transported to a meeting point for a debriefing, followed by a final group meeting.
LEARNING OUTCOME ASSESSMENT: Students completed a questionnaire at the beginning and end of the activity, including technical and subjective questions about perceived preparedness. Statistical analysis used the Chi-square test to compare response frequencies. 112 fifth-year medical students completed the online questionnaire.
RESULTS: Seventy-one pre-activity and 41 post-activity questionnaires were completed. Perceived preparedness significantly improved: initially, 66.2% felt "no" prepared, which decreased to 4.9% after the activity (p < 0.001). Correct responses to "first thing to do in an attack" increased from 19.4% to 92.7% (p < 0.001). Understanding "improvised means" rose from 85.9% to 100% (p = 0.042). No statistically significant differences were observed for more technical questions like hemorrhage or cardiac arrest.
DISCUSSION: Teaching through simulated environments offers undeniable learning benefits. While curriculum integration faces, simulation is a valuable tool in emergency training. Our cost-effective instructional methods proved successful, as shown by survey data. These engaging experiences facilitate knowledge acquisition. Replicating real-life conditions helps students appreciate inherent challenges. We conclude that using a simulated environment at the undergraduate level to train students as first responders in mass casualty incidents is an effective educational strategy.

articles.title: Growing Proficiency in Tic Disorder Care and Skills (GP-TiCS): a thematic analysis of patient and professional group experiences in primary care for primary tic disorders.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Around 300,000 people in the UK are thought to be living with Tourette syndrome (TS). Many people with tics and their families report negative experiences when approaching their general practitioner (GP) for advice and support. Limited education during medical training coupled with a lack of National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines for tic disorders (TD) creates clinical challenges for healthcare professionals (HCPs). Building on the results of an international systematic review of healthcare experiences for tics, this study aimed to further explore patient and professional experiences in primary care in England, specifically.
METHODS: A thematic analysis was conducted on interviews with adults with tics (n = 5), parents of children and young people (CYP) with tics (n = 5), GPs (n = 6), and secondary care HCPs working with people with tics (n = 4).
RESULTS: The Factors Impacting GPs' Knowledge and Education of Tics theme suggested that limited education and guidance made it more difficult for GPs to support people presenting with tics yet also considers how surmounting pressures and expectations on primary care may exceed the responsibility and capabilities of GPs. Inconsistent Availability of Support for Tics Across the Country continues to be an issue for GPs making referrals to services and for people seeking support, while secondary HCPs report receiving unclear referrals with limited information which makes service allocation more difficult. The Experiences of Primary Care for Tics theme explores how the wider impact of living with tics is often left unexplored, while stigma, communication, and signposting were all identified areas for improvement.
CONCLUSION: The results suggest accessible and appropriate education opportunities for GPs may improve experience for people presenting with tics by increasing GP knowledge and awareness of tics. This study precedes the development of an online learning resource for GPs.

articles.title: Medical Students' Experience of Death and Near-Death of a "Patient" During Simulation: A Qualitative Study.
articles.journal: Simulation in healthcare : journal of the Society for Simulation in Healthcare
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: This study explores medical students' perceived learning, emotional responses, and sense of preparedness following simulated death and near-death scenarios to understand how learners interpret these emotionally challenging simulation experiences. Simulation-based medical education empowers students to develop clinical skills in a safe environment, including dealing with critical scenarios involving a patient's death. While these simulations may evoke intense emotional responses, they may also provide thought-provoking learning experiences that promote deeper reflection and introspection.
METHODS: We adopted an interpretative qualitative approach. Thirteen final-year medical students were recruited using a purposive sampling technique. They were exposed to simulation sessions involving death and near-death using a high-fidelity manikin. A semistructured interview was conducted, and the data were analyzed using thematic analysis. The trustworthiness of the data was ensured through credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability criteria.
RESULTS: Five main themes emerged from simulation experiences, i.e emotional responses to simulated death, learning through simulated death, impact on motivation, realism and immersion, and challenges during simulated death. Participants described emotions such as sadness, guilt, and acceptance of death as part of the learning process. Simulation-based learning provided a platform for self-reflection, empathy, safe practice, and preparation for real-life scenarios. Challenges such as limited knowledge and skills, difficulties in leadership and teamwork, and emotional management were identified as subthemes within the challenges theme.
CONCLUSION: Simulated death may prompt emotional, motivational, and professional reflection among students, while also revealing the need for stronger educational support within simulation-based training. Incorporating structured debriefing and psychological support could help learners better navigate emotionally complex simulation experiences.

articles.title: "An Even Playing Field": Non-Clinical Simulation for Leadership Development Among Pediatric Interns.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Graduate training programs are tasked with preparing trainees to lead clinical teams. Currently, there is little consensus on how to develop their interpersonal leadership skills, and pediatric programs tend to focus on senior residents. Targeting pediatric interns with strategies for developing interpersonal leadership skills provides more opportunity to consolidate and apply these skills during training.
OBJECTIVE: We aimed to understand how simulation facilitates the development of interpersonal leadership skills among pediatric interns.
METHODS: Pediatric interns participated in an outdoor wilderness simulation repeated 4 times between July-November 2022. The simulation and debrief focused on consensus decision-making and communication. To explore if and how simulation outside of clinical teams and devoid of clinical content fostered interpersonal leadership skills, we conducted semi-structured focus groups after each debrief. We conducted thematic analysis of the recorded debriefs and focus groups.
RESULTS: Forty nine of 53 eligible interns participated. Participants demonstrated learning about interpersonal leadership skills and began to build a leadership identity. Simulation facilitated this development through 3 core elements. Detaching the simulation from clinical content and settings leveled the playing field and engendered experimentation and examination. Despite this separation, the simulation prompted participants to link to clinical spaces through reflection on translating interpersonal leadership skills to clinical settings.
CONCLUSION: Simulation outside of clinical teams and free of clinical content creates safe spaces for pediatric interns to develop interpersonal leadership skills. Earlier acquisition of these skills may facilitate leadership development over the course of pediatric training.

articles.title: Opportunities and barriers in health education and community awareness program: a qualitative study from Indian tertiary care teaching hospital.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Health education is an important public health intervention that promotes disease prevention, awareness generation, and healthy behavioural practices within communities. Undergraduate medical students are increasingly involved in community-based health education activities; however, they often encounter several operational and communication-related challenges during field implementation. This study explored the perceptions of undergraduate medical students regarding the challenges and opportunities in imparting health education in community settings.
METHODS: A phenomenological qualitative study was conducted among third-year undergraduate medical students in the Department of Community Medicine and Family Medicine at All India Institute of Medical Sciences Bhubaneswar between July 2022 and October 2022. Participants were selected through purposive sampling after attending health education training and participating in community-based health education activities. In-depth interviews were conducted using a semi-structured interview guide. Data saturation was achieved after nine interviews; additional interviews were conducted to improve data richness. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed thematically using ATLAS.ti.
RESULTS: A total of fifteen undergraduate medical students participated in the study. Participants perceived health education as an important tool for improving community awareness, preventive healthcare, and medication adherence. Interactive methods such as skits, role-plays, posters, demonstrations, and local-language communication were considered effective in enhancing community engagement. Major challenges identified included language barriers, inadequate training, limited institutional support, logistical constraints, poor community participation, and excessive workload among community mobilizers. Students emphasized that collaboration with ASHA workers and community mobilizers improved rapport building and public participation. Opportunities identified included stronger faculty mentorship, better planning, culturally sensitive communication, community-centred educational strategies, and enhanced institutional and community support.
CONCLUSION: Undergraduate medical students recognized the importance of health education in improving community health; however, several communication, organisational and logistical barriers affected its implementation in community settings. Strengthening community-oriented medical education, local-language communication skills, faculty mentorship, and collaboration with community mobilizers may improve the effectiveness and sustainability of community health education programmes.

articles.title: Rewriting professional identity: a self-authorship perspective on neurodivergent learners in health professions education.
articles.journal: Advances in health sciences education : theory and practice
articles.abstract: Professional identity formation in health professions education is often conceptualised as socialisation into established professional norms and values. For neurodivergent learners, however, these norms may reflect assumptions that privilege neurotypical ways of thinking, communicating, and behaving. While professional identity formation has been explored among other minoritised learners, less is known about how neurodivergent learners navigate this process. This study explored how neurodivergent graduates of Australian health professions programs constructed professional identities. Twelve neurodivergent health professionals participated in semi-structured interviews or provided written responses. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, informed by Baxter Magolda's theory of self-authorship. Participants initially encountered narrow archetypes of the "ideal health professional" that were shaped by assumptions about capability, professionalism, and neurotypical behaviour. These expectations generated identity dissonance, concerns about disclosure, and pressure to mask neurodivergent traits. Over time, participants developed greater self-recognition of their strengths, needs, and preferred ways of practising. This enabled them to critically question dominant constructions of professionalism and to rework professional identities in ways that were more authentic, sustainable, and aligned with their values. Rather than simply assimilating into existing norms, participants actively expanded and reshaped understandings of what competent and compassionate healthcare practice can look like. Viewed through the lens of self-authorship, these findings highlight how professional identity formation for neurodivergent learners involves negotiating, resisting, and reconstructing professional norms. In response, educators could move beyond supporting learners to conform to dominant professional archetypes and instead create educational environments that recognise diverse ways of being, foster self-authorship, and broaden understandings of professionalism within the health professions.

articles.title: What Matters Most to Students in Simulation-Based Education: Voices from Three Philippine State Universities.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Simulation-based education (SBE) has expanded in Philippine health professions programs, particularly among state universities and colleges (SUCs) supported by national and institutional capacity-building initiatives. Despite this growth, limited local evidence describes how Filipino students experience and learn through simulation across varying institutional contexts.
OBJECTIVE: This study explored undergraduate dentistry, medicine, and nursing students' experiences of SBE in SUCs and examined how simulation influenced their learning and professional development.
METHODS: An exploratory-descriptive qualitative study was conducted in three SUCs representing academic programs in which SBE ranged from newly implemented to well integrated. Purposive sampling recruited students with substantive participation in simulation activities. Eight focus group discussions (n = 47) were conducted using a semi-structured guide informed by Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory. Data were analyzed through inductive qualitative content analysis within a constructivist approach, with paired coding, iterative comparison, and team consensus to generate themes. The Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) were followed in the writing of this paper.
RESULTS: Across institutions, students described SBE as a structured, psychologically safe learning space that strengthened clinical reasoning, communication, teamwork, and reflective practice. Authenticity of scenarios, faculty facilitation, and structured debriefing were central to meaningful learning. Differences in institutional resources and program maturity influenced perceived realism and depth of engagement. Students highlighted simulation's role in building confidence and bridging theory to practice within resource-variable contexts.
CONCLUSIONS: In Philippine SUCs, SBE supports experiential learning processes that enhance cognitive, affective, and collaborative competencies among undergraduate health professions students. Sustained institutional investment in faculty development, scenario design, and reflective debriefing is essential to ensure equitable and high-quality simulation implementation across diverse public higher education settings.

articles.title: Exploration of best practices in the creation and dissemination of video vignettes in mental healthcare training: a qualitative analysis of multiple stakeholder perspectives across US psychosis services.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Video vignettes are widely used in mental and physical healthcare training, yet limited guidelines exist on best practices for their creation and use, particularly with regard to the meaningful and respectful inclusion of lived experience. This study is the first to qualitatively examine this topic from multiple stakeholder perspectives, using psychosis care as the case example.
DESIGN: 6 qualitative focus groups and 1 written response were analysed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis.
SETTING: Across the USA.
PARTICIPANTS: 3 stakeholder groups were recruited: trainers who use video vignettes (n=9), trainees whose training has included the use of video vignettes (n=9) and people who self-identified as having lived experience of psychosis (n=10). Three individuals identified with and took part in more than one group.
RESULTS: 4 overarching themes were identified: (1) video vignettes as both powerful and problematic tools, (2) balancing differences in expectations and purposes of video vignettes, (3) ethical tensions in how to represent lived experience and (4) tools to support more ethical and collaborative practices. While diverse perspectives emerged, clear priorities for improvement were identified. These included prioritising advance planning, defining the purpose of the video vignette and using iterative development, providing transparency and contextualisation about videos during training, nuanced management of privacy and consent and including lived experience perspectives throughout the process with appropriate support. A summary box of recommendations is provided in the text.
CONCLUSIONS: Video vignettes can have significant training value, but there is a need for ethical, collaborative and consistent practices around their creation and dissemination in order to minimise the perpetuation of stigma. The most consistent finding was that lived experience expertise can be harnessed at every stage throughout the process of both creating and using video vignettes in order to reduce stigma and enhance learning. Implications extend beyond training mental health providers to healthcare education more broadly.

articles.title: Experiential teaching centered on science popularisation videos: a randomised controlled trial on the impact on learning outcomes and core competencies of dental preventive medicine students.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medical students, as key communicators of health information in the future, require high-quality education and training. Traditional teaching models, which primarily focus on theoretical instruction, have limitations in cultivating students' mastery of knowledge and their health education competencies. Experiential teaching, characterized by active learning and practical participation, offers new perspectives for medical education reform. However, existing studies have largely focused on the effectiveness of video viewing as a pedagogical medium, and there remains a lack of high-quality empirical research evaluating the specific impact of experiential teaching centered on science popularisation video production on students' learning outcomes and core competencies.
METHOD: This study initially enrolled 80 undergraduate students from the compulsory course Oral Preventive Medicine, with 72 in the final analysis. Using a computer-generated randomization sequence, students were allocated at a 1:1 ratio to an intervention group or a control group (36 each), with assessors blinded to group assignment. The control group received conventional lecture-based instruction and post-class readings; the intervention group additionally participated in a health education video production project grounded in Kolb's experiential learning theory. Intervention effectiveness was assessed through a multidimensional system comprising a theoretical knowledge test, a self-assessment competency scale, a structured video quality scoring sheet, and a course experience questionnaire.
RESULT: After the intervention, the intervention group showed significantly higher theoretical knowledge scores than the control group ([Formula: see text] vs. [Formula: see text], [Formula: see text], [Formula: see text], Partial [Formula: see text]). The self-perceived core competency total score was also significantly higher in the intervention group than in the control group ([Formula: see text] vs. [Formula: see text], [Formula: see text], [Formula: see text], Partial [Formula: see text], adjusted [Formula: see text]). The overall quality rating of the intervention group's popular science videos was [Formula: see text] (out of 5), with creativity and communication appeal scoring the highest ([Formula: see text]). Course feedback revealed that the intervention group scored significantly higher than the control group on key items including knowledge translation, planning and design, communication confidence, and career development perception (all [Formula: see text], Cohen's [Formula: see text]-2.35).
CONCLUSION: Experiential teaching centered on science popularisation video production not only significantly improved dental preventive medicine students' mastery of theoretical knowledge and self-perceived core health education competencies, but also yielded popular science works of satisfactory quality, suggesting that this teaching model positively promotes students' learning outcomes and core competencies, while profoundly strengthening their recognition of curriculum content and professional identity.

articles.title: Staff experiences of a newly developed blended learning program to improve diabetes management at orthopedic clinics.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Errors in diabetes treatment are among the most frequently reported adverse events in hospitals and orthopaedic care. This study aimed to identify the learning needs of orthopaedic staff, develop a blended diabetes learning programme, and examine orthopaedic staff experiences of participating in the programme.
METHODS: Nurses and physicians from endocrinological and orthopedic wards at three hospitals in the capital region of Denmark (Bispebjerg, Herlev, Nordsjællands Hospitals) participated in group concept mapping. A total of 193 orthopedic staffmembers completed an e-learning module and 174 attended one of 12 face-to-face classes. We used thematic analysis to analyze data from four focus group interviews (n = 14 nurses) and observations from face-to-face classes.
RESULTS: We identified 12 learning objectives and identified three overall themes from thematic analysis: learning through cases, combining e-learning and face-to-face courses, and from learning to practice. These themes explained processes and contexts that facilitated or inhibited learning.
CONCLUSIONS: This study identified several key contexts (time, place, level of knowledge, nurse seniority, organisational support) and critical processes (educators' facilitation, scaffolding, case-based learning) that influence physicians and nurses learning experience and applying it in practice.

articles.title: Exploring perspectives and engagement in space surgery: a survey of SAGES members.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: SAGES' space surgery task force was created in 2023 in response to the potential increased need for surgical intervention in space as humanity seeks to establish larger and more permanent populations in space environments. This task force sought to assess the needs, limitations, and anticipated challenges of surgical care in space environments and to offer leadership opportunities by surveying the SAGES membership.
METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional survey of the SAGES membership soliciting respondent's experience in aerospace medicine and related fields, as well as members' interests within space surgery and their opinions about the future surgical needs of space explorers. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographics, interests, and preferences, and narrative review and thematic analysis were used to analyze open-ended responses.
RESULTS: Survey response rate was 6.1%. Most respondents were attending minimally invasive or general surgeons. Experience was reported in telehealth, artificial intelligence, austere environment surgery, and military medicine. Greatest interest was expressed in the application of robotic technologies in space. Respondents wished to participate in technical skills workshops and to view presentations by astronauts on space medicine as part of the future activities of the task force at SAGES annual meetings. Themes identified as challenges to space surgery included microgravity, resource limitations, remote surgery, training, and specific medical concerns. Future areas of focus included technology and innovation, protocol/system design, adjustment to medical standards, and training programs.
CONCLUSION: This survey identified a strong interest among the SAGES membership in leading the conversation surrounding space surgery as humanity expands beyond low earth orbit. Numerous opportunities, challenges, and new directions were identified by respondents that will guide the future activities of the task force.

articles.title: Not just what is taught, but how it is lived: socially accountable education in health professions education.
articles.journal: Advances in health sciences education : theory and practice
articles.abstract: Social accountability (SA) is a defining institutional mandate in health professions education (HPE), yet how educational approaches associated with SA are experienced in practice remains insufficiently understood. Rather than examining what these approaches aim to achieve, this study explores how they are encountered, interpreted, and made meaningful by those directly involved. We conducted an interpretive descriptive study using rich picture interviews combined with semi-structured interviews with 46 participants, including learners, clinical teachers, community organization members, patient partners, and leaders in SA. Participants depicted and discussed their experiences with educational approaches related to SA. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Five interrelated themes were identified. Participants described (a) an evolving reorientation in how they understood and positioned themselves in relation to responsibility, (b) the limits of abstraction, where experiential encounters revealed dissonance between lived realities and curricular representations, (c) reflexivity as uneven and pedagogically mediated, requiring dialogue, continuity, and psychological safety, (d) institutional conditions as shaping what can be questioned or enacted, including hierarchy, role modeling, and competing priorities, and (e) social accountability as a collective and relational practice, in which participation, reciprocity, and whose perspectives shape educational processes mattered. Across these themes, the presence of an educational approach did not itself determine how socially accountable education was experienced or made meaningful. Meaning was shaped through the interplay between what encounters made visible, opportunities to interpret and question those experiences, the institutional conditions in which they occurred, and whose perspectives were able to shape the educational process. Advancing SA in HPE therefore requires attention not only to which educational approaches are included, but to how they are experienced, facilitated, and negotiated within educational and community relationships.

articles.title: The Palette and the Playground: Reflexive Thematic Analysis as Interpretive Art and Courageous Play.
articles.abstract: Drawing on sustained engagement with reflexive thematic analysis (RTA) across health professions education and health systems research within an academic health system in the Arabian Gulf, this commentary explores what becomes visible when RTA is practiced not merely as a procedural framework but as an interpretive sensibility. Rather than revisiting Braun and Clarke's familiar six-phase framework of RTA, the paper reflects on how RTA functions across mixed-methods inquiry, iterative implementation work, conceptual framework development, and contextually grounded qualitative research. Two conceptual provocations are offered. The first reframes thematic interpretation through the metaphor of colour mixing, proposing that themes are analyst-generated hues selected from a theoretically expansive interpretive spectrum. The second draws on Peter Gray's theory of free play to conceptualise reflexivity as a form of courageous intellectual play. Together, these provocations argue for a methodological vocabulary that positions interpretation as reflexive, creative, and theory-situated work, rather than procedural extraction, whether that 'theory' is a named framework or the analyst's own inductive, constructivist engagement with the data.

articles.title: Educating, Administrating, Promoting, and Evaluating: The Roles of Health Professions Education Community of Practice Facilitators.
articles.abstract: Communities of Practice (CoP) are a model for faculty development in health professions education (HPE) that focuses on continuous improvement and a culture of shared responsibility. CoP facilitators are integral to the development and sustainability of CoPs. The researchers examined the experiences of HPE CoP facilitators by identifying their tasks, challenges, and strategies for overcoming barriers to guide CoP facilitation. Researchers engaged in a qualitative study of their own CoP facilitator experiences (n = 5) that were collected through a collaborative reflective inquiry using question prompts for guided reflection. Responses were examined utilising iterative thematic analysis in four phases. Positionality and reflexivity were considered through ongoing discussion among the research team. Four themes emerged to describe the responsibilities of CoP facilitators: Educator, Administrator, Promoter, and Evaluator. Challenges for facilitators included time, scheduling, defining participation and engagement, planning content, lack of formalised incentives, and measuring outcomes. Challenges were addressed by creating opportunities for asynchronous engagement, flexibility to meet the needs of participants, valuing and celebrating efforts rather than only outcomes, and focusing on the importance of CoPs. Our findings identified key roles and tasks of CoP facilitators which, when grouped into "before", "during", and "after" categories, provided a tool to specify the work facilitators may expect when developing, sustaining, and communicating about CoPs. These findings add facilitator-specific guidance, complementing previous work describing general CoP phases. The barriers identified within this study build upon those found in CoP literature within HPE and suggest contributors to sustainability.
